sens: without valid foundation, without legitimate reason
without useful result, fruitlessly
in a hollow, superficial manner
G1500.detail:
1. Without valid foundation, without legitimate reason: when one acts or speaks without just cause. In Matthew 5:22, Jesus says that being angry with one's brother "without cause" (that is, unjustifiably) exposes one to condemnation.

2. Without useful result, fruitlessly: when an effort, suffering, or belief leads to nothing lasting. In 1 Corinthians 15:2, Paul warns that believing the message of Christ "in vain" would mean deriving no salvation from it. In Galatians 3:4 and 4:11, suffering or working "in vain" for the Church means laboring without seeing any fruit.

3. In a hollow, superficial manner: when something lacks true substance. In Colossians 2:18, "vain pride" based on carnal thoughts is a pride without solid foundation, which inflates the ego without building up. In Romans 13:4, the magistrate's sword is not borne "in vain": it has a true function, to exercise justice.
G1500.origine: The Greek word eikē comes from a root meaning "image" or "appearance." This is why it carries the idea of something that is hollow, lacking real substance, something that has only appearance. The word literally designates what lacks a solid foundation, true reason, or what produces no tangible effect. This etymology explains why it qualifies both an act without cause and an effort without result.
G1500.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the Gospel of Matthew. In Matthew 5:22, it characterizes an unjustified anger. In Paul, it mainly describes efforts, sufferings, or beliefs that fail to produce fruit: this is the case in 1 Corinthians 15:2 (believing without persevering would be useless), in Galatians 3:4 and 4:11 (apostolic work that does not yield results), and in Romans 13:4 (the sword that would not be borne "in vain," meaning it truly fulfills its function). In Colossians 2:18, it applies to empty pride. The word always targets inefficiency, a lack of foundation or real result.
G1500.portee: This word reminds Christians that faith is not hollow: it must be rooted in the truth of Christ and produce lasting fruit. It warns against superficial religious efforts, words without cause, and unfounded pride. It also invites us to check that our commitment to God is not sterile, but that it bears fruit in our lives and in the lives of others.

sens: The whole number 20, formed of two groups of ten
G1501.detail: 1. The number 20 designates a specific quantity, often used for concrete enumerations: soldiers (Luke 14:31: "twenty thousand"), a depth measured in fathoms (Acts 27:28), gathered people (Acts 1:15: "about one hundred twenty"), or celestial beings in vision (Revelation 4:4: "twenty-four elders"). It is a useful number for expressing precise or approximate quantities in everyday life and in prophetic visions.
G1501.origine: The Greek word εἴκοσι comes from a common ancient Indo-European root found in several languages to denote this number. It has no variable form ("indeclinable"): it remains the same regardless of its use in the sentence. It is a pure numeral term, with no etymological link to other biblical words.
G1501.emploi: This word appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts, Revelation, and the Gospels. It is used to count soldiers in comparison (Luke 14:31), to measure marine distances (John 6:19: "twenty-five or thirty stadia"), to number a group (Acts 1:15), to probe the depth of the sea (Acts 27:28), and especially to enumerate celestial creatures in John's visions (Revelation 4:4, 10; 5:8; 11:16; 19:4: "twenty-four elders"). The number 24 regularly recurs as a symbolic number of the heavenly assembly.

sens: To yield to pressure, constraint, or order
Not to bend in the face of opposition
G1502.detail:
1. The verb εἴκω primarily means to yield, bend, or submit to pressure or constraint: it conveys the idea of letting go. In Galatians 2:5, Paul says, "we did not yield to them for a moment," which means he did not bend to the false apostles who wanted to impose circumcision on non-Jewish converts.
2. By extension, the word takes on the meaning of resisting, holding firm, refusing to yield — the opposite of the first idea. This is the sense it has in the Segond, which translates as "to resist": Paul and his companions stood firm on the truth of the Gospel despite external pressures.
G1502.origine: The verb εἴκω comes from a Greek root expressing the idea of yielding or collapsing. There is a Greek variant ὑπείκω (hypeikô), "to yield under the weight of," which reinforces this image of weakness or capitulation. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew ענה (ânâh), which means to respond or submit, showing how the concept of "yielding" relates to acceptance or submission.
G1502.emploi: εἴκω appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 2:5. Paul recounts how he refused to yield to the demands of the false apostles who wanted to compel Titus to be circumcised. The context is one of a firm defense of the truth of the Gospel against legalistic pressures. The sense of "to resist" (not to yield) is here obtained by negation: "we did not yield," which means "we held firm." This rarity of usage contrasts with more common words like ἀντίστημι (anthistèmi) to express resistance.
G1502.portee: This word reminds the reader that fidelity to the truth of the Gospel sometimes requires holding firm despite pressures and criticisms. Paul shows that yielding on a central point — here salvation by grace alone — would have compromised the integrity of the Christian message. It is a lesson on the cost of faithfulness and the importance of not bending to compromises that would distort the faith.

sens: To be similar to someone or something
To have the appearance or nature of
G1503.detail:
1. To resemble means to have the same characteristics, appearance, or nature as another person or thing. It establishes a comparison between two realities to show that they are alike. In James 1:6, the one who doubts resembles the wave of the sea tossed by the wind: just as the waves are tossed about, the man without certainty is unstable and inconsistent in his faith.
2. This word also expresses an analogy or similarity of condition. In James 1:23, the one who listens to the word without putting it into practice resembles a man who looks at himself in a mirror and then goes away forgetting what he looks like: he has knowledge that produces no change in him.
G1503.origine: The verb εἴκω comes from an Indo-European root expressing the idea of "to resemble" or "to be similar." It is related to the form ἔοικα, which in the Septuagint often translates the Hebrew verb דָּמָה (damah), which literally means "to be comparable" or "to be in the same order." This verb belongs to a small family of Greek words expressing similarity and comparison.
G1503.emploi: The verb εἴκω is very rare in the New Testament: it appears only twice, both in the epistle of James. In James 1:6 and 1:23, it introduces comparisons that structure James's argument on authentic faith. In both cases, the verb establishes a parallel between a spiritual attitude (doubt, forgetting what one has heard) and a visible concrete reality (the wave of the sea, the mirror). These comparisons are not superficial judgments: they reveal the deep nature of the problem. Doubt makes a person unstable; forgetfulness makes them ineffective.
G1503.portee: This word shows us that our actions and attitudes have an inner coherence: we resemble what we do. If we doubt, we become like agitated water, without stability. If we listen without obeying, we deceive ourselves. James uses these images to call us to integrity: our faith must transform our lives, otherwise we are merely reflections without reality.

sens: Visible representation or portrait of a person or thing
Engraved or stamped effigy on a coin or object
Reflection or appearance that manifests the reality of an original
Resemblance of one person to another, particularly that of a child to a parent
Idolatrous representation or statue worshiped as a god
Visible manifestation and expression of the nature or character of a person
G1504.detail:
1. The primary meaning is a visual representation: an image is what makes a person or thing visible and recognizable. When Jesus asks the disciples whose effigy is engraved on a coin (Matthew 22:20), he is literally speaking of the printed image of the sovereign.
2. In particular, an effigy is the official portrait engraved or stamped on objects like coins. This is the most concrete meaning of the word in the context of the temple: Caesar's effigy bears the inscription of his name (Mark 12:16).
3. An image can also refer to the reflection or visible manifestation of something invisible or greater. The image differs from a mere reflection or shadow: it implies that there exists an original of which it is a faithful reproduction (Hebrews 10:1).
4. In personal relationships, the image can signify the resemblance between two beings, such as that of a child resembling a parent. Paul speaks of bearing the image of the earthly and then that of the heavenly (1 Corinthians 15:49), meaning progressing in a transformation that makes us similar.
5. An image can also be a material representation that is worshiped, a statue or object of idolatrous worship. Revelation mentions the beast and its image, which designates a representation before which one bows down and worships (Revelation 13:14).
6. Finally, the word expresses how a person visibly manifests or expresses the character or glory of another. Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), meaning that he manifests and makes visible the nature, glory, and authority of the Father.
G1504.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to be similar" or "to resemble." It fundamentally designates what is similar to something else and represents it. The image is not a mere accidental copy: it implies an intentional link with an original or archetype — like the effigy of a king on a coin reveals and represents the king himself. The Hebrew word it often translates in the Greek Old Testament is צֶלֶם (selem), which literally means "form" or "figure." This word appears as early as Genesis when man is created "in the image of God."
G1504.emploi: The word appears 20 times in the provided usages, primarily in the Pauline epistles and Revelation. In the Gospels, it refers to the material effigy on coins (Matthew 22:20, Mark 12:16, Luke 20:24). Paul uses it to express the relationship between God and man: man is created in the image of God (1 Corinthians 11:7), the regenerated believer is renewed in the image of God (Colossians 3:10), and must progress toward the image of the Son of God (Romans 8:29, 2 Corinthians 3:18). It is also a powerful Christological term: Christ is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15, 2 Corinthians 4:4), expressing his divine nature and function of revelation. In Revelation, the word takes on a negative sense: the image of the beast refers to the statues or idolatrous representations that are worshiped (Revelation 13:14-15, 14:9-11, 19:20, 20:4).
G1504.portee: This word reveals the central place of resemblance to God in God's design for man. By learning that man is created in the image of God, the Christian understands his dignity and responsibility before his Creator. By seeing Christ presented as the perfect image of the invisible God, he contemplates the total revelation of God and understands who Jesus truly is. The progressive transformation of the believer into the image of Christ becomes a living call: our destiny is to become increasingly similar to Jesus, manifesting his glory in our lives. This word reminds us that true resemblance to God does not reside in material images or idols, but in an inner and moral transformation.

sens: Absence of mixture or alteration
Moral integrity and absence of duplicity
Sincerity of heart and word
G1505.detail:
1. The word first evokes something pure, without mixture. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 5:8 when he speaks of the "unleavened bread of purity": just as leaven corrupts the dough, malice corrupts the heart, and purity is the absence of that corruption.
2. Moral purity means not deceiving or disguising one's intentions. In 2 Corinthians 1:12, Paul asserts that he has conducted himself "with purity before God": this means he has hidden nothing, falsified nothing in his dealings with the Corinthians — no hidden calculations, no double dealing.
3. Sincerity is honesty without pretense in speech. When Paul says in 2 Corinthians 2:17 that he speaks "with sincerity," he contrasts with those who "distort the word of God": he speaks the truth without adapting it to please or for his profit.
G1505.origine: The word comes from an image: literally "judged in the light of the sun" (from the ancient Greek *heile*, sun, and *krinein*, to judge). It is what can withstand examination in full light, without fear of uncovering a pretense. This word belongs to the family of Greek words that speak of discernment and judgment.
G1505.emploi: Paul uses this word only three times in his epistles, and always to speak of his own conduct or that which he commands. In 1 Corinthians 5:8, purity characterizes the redemptive people who turn away from malice. In 2 Corinthians 1:12 and 2:17, it is the quality of one who, in the face of accusations of dishonesty, can affirm his integrity before God: Paul defends himself by showing that his conscience, God bears witness, that his conduct and his word are transparent.
G1505.portee: This word calls the Christian to total transparency before God and before men. No double bottom, no hidden intentions, no disguised words — it is a sincerity that even invites God himself as a witness. It is only possible by grace and requires courage, as it rejects the twisted paths of lies or calculation.

sens: Not mixed, without alloy or impurity
Clear and limpid in essence
Intact, without moral defect
G1506.detail:
1. The word evokes a substance without mixture, like pure gold without alloy (from which the Latin word "sincerus" comes). In Philippians 1:10, Paul wishes that believers be "pure," meaning without mixture of guilt or hypocrisy on the day of judgment.
2. It can designate what is clear and transparent in its nature: a "sound" mind (2 Peter 3:1) is a thought free from troubles, lucid, not clouded by errors or passions.
3. On a moral and ethical level, the word describes one whose heart and intentions are free from any mixture of evil, whose conscience is clear. It is purity not only ritual but also internal.
G1506.origine: The Greek word comes from an ancient image: the sun shining without clouds, clear and without mixture. It is related to Greek words meaning "to judge" and "to cut." The same root has given rise to Latin words like "sincerus" (sincere), which evokes absolute purity, without deceit.
G1506.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Philippians 1:10, Paul applies it to the spiritual condition of believers: they must be "pure and blameless" on the day of Christ, meaning without conscious guilt. In 2 Peter 3:1, he qualifies the "mind" or Christian thought: it must be "sound," preserved from confusion and false teachings. In both cases, it is a complete purity, without mixture of evil or error.
G1506.portee: This word reminds the Christian that moral and mental purity is a spiritual goal. It is not primarily an outward appearance, but an integrity of heart and thought, free from hypocrisy and trouble. Aspiring to be "pure" means allowing the Holy Spirit to clarify and unify our conscience, intentions, and faith.

sens: To exist, to have a concrete reality
To be located somewhere, to be present in a place
To happen, to occur, to take place
To belong to someone, to be their property or character
To constitute, to form the identity of something (in a statement)
To identify with, to become (in a context of transformation or equivalence)
G1510.detail:
1. The simplest meaning: to exist, to have a reality. It is to be there, to subsist. John asserts that the Word "is" from the beginning (John 1:1). When Paul says that we "are" children of God (Romans 8:16), he expresses a new existence acquired through faith.

2. To be physically present somewhere. Jesus "is" in a place, his disciples "are" gathered. Mark recounts: "There was a man possessed by a demon" (Mark 5:21). This simply indicates where something or someone is located.

3. To occur, to happen, to take place in time. Events "are": the Passover "is" near (Mark 14:2), a famine "has" come (Acts 11:28). The word describes what happens or what is taking place.

4. To belong to, to be the property or attribute of someone. Jesus says to God: "Yours is the kingdom, the power, and the glory" (Matthew 6:13). This indicates who possesses or has such a quality.

5. To identify something through the attributive verb "to be": "I am the way" (John 14:6). Here, the verb unites the subject to an attribute that completely defines it. It is to establish an equivalence or an identity statement.

6. In parable or interpretative narratives, to establish a figurative correspondence: "This represents that" or "means." Matthew 13:19: "the seed is the word" ("ἐστιν" establishes the equation).
G1510.origine: The verb εἰμί (eimi) is the fundamental verb "to be" in Greek, with no apparent root — it is a primitive verb found in all Indo-European languages (compare with French "être," German "sein"). Its etymology dates back to the earliest layer of the language. In Hebrew and Aramaic, the corresponding verb is הָיָה (hayah) or הֲוָה (hawah), which express both existence and presence. This root appears in biblical names: Jehovah, the divine name, is built on this same root ("I am that I am," Exodus 3:14). The Greek verb has borrowed from the inflection of the Hebrew verb its nuances: to exist, to be present, to happen, to belong.
G1510.emploi: The verb εἰμί is the most frequent in the New Testament: 2039 occurrences counted! It appears everywhere. As a substantive verb ("to be"), it states existence or presence: "There is a rich man" (Luke 16:19), "we are children of God" (Romans 8:16). As a copula (linking verb), it unites a subject to an attribute to identify or qualify: "You are the salt of the earth" (Matthew 5:13), "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12). It can also express belonging or possession: "Yours is... the kingdom and the power" (Matthew 6:13). Finally, with participles, it forms compound tenses to express a continuous or past action: "Jesus taught with authority" (Matthew 7:29, literally "Jesus was teaching"). Its use varies finely according to context, but the meaning is always related to existence, presence, or identity.
G1510.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb carries major theological depth. When Jesus says "I am" without an attribute (John 8:58), he asserts himself with the very name of God revealed to Moses. The verb "to be" thus becomes the expression of divine eternity, of absolute existence. For the believer, being "in Christ" or being "a child of God" is not a mere moral statement: it is an ontological identity, a radical transformation of one's being. The humble verb "to be" actually states that our existence is redefined by grace.

sens: To exist, to have a present reality
To be located in a place, to be present
To happen, to take place, to occur
To serve as, to play the role of (linking verb)
To constitute the essence or identity of something
To remain, to stay in a state or condition
G1511.detail: 1. The verb expresses simple existence, the fact that a person or thing is real (John 17:5: "before the world existed," the world had an existence). 2. It marks presence in a place: someone or something is located at a given spot (Luke 8:38: the man asks for permission to "stay" with Jesus, meaning to remain close to him). 3. The verb also means that an action or event occurs, happens at a specific moment (Luke 2:6: "while they were there," the time for the birth came). 4. Very often, it functions as a link between a subject and its description: it connects what a person or thing truly is (1 Timothy 2:12: the woman must "remain" silent expresses a state that she must maintain). 5. It can also mean the deep essence or what truly constitutes something (Romans 6:11: "consider yourselves dead to sin" means consider yourselves as having that nature). 6. Finally, it expresses maintaining a condition, a permanent state: to stay or remain in a way of being (Galatians 2:9: those who "are regarded as pillars" maintain this central role in the community).
G1511.origine: This Greek verb is one of the oldest and most fundamental words in Greek. It comes from a very ancient Indo-European root (Sanskrit "as-", Latin "esse"). In biblical Greek, it often translates the Hebrew "hayah" (היה), which literally means "to become" or "to happen." The verb carries the idea of real presence and effective existence: what "is" has a tangible reality, unlike what exists only in imagination.
G1511.emploi: This verb appears more than 2000 times in the entire New Testament, including about 124 times in the listed passages. It is used in all books and contexts: it is absolutely fundamental. Sometimes it simply means to exist or to be there (Acts 2:12: "What does this mean?" raises the question of what is happening). Other times it serves as a simple copula, linking a subject to its description (Romans 1:20: "his invisible attributes are clearly seen in creation"). In some passages, especially in the Gospel of John, it carries a strong theological weight: John favors absolute existence statements where Jesus says "I am" to affirm his divine nature (John 4:26). The verb can also express the idea of staying or persisting in a place or state (1 Corinthians 7:32: "without concern"). Its versatility makes it a crucial word for all biblical theology.
G1511.portee: This simple yet profound verb invites the reader to meditate on the reality of existence: God is, Jesus is, and everything that exists derives its being from him. When the Gospel of John uses "I am," it asserts that Jesus is not an abstraction but a real and living person. This verb also raises the question of the meaning of our actions: are we truly what we believe we are, or merely what we are commanded to become in Christ? It is a call to examine our existence in the light of the very existence of God.

sens: Be at peace with one another, without conflict
Maintain concord and harmony within a community
Cultivate inner and relational tranquility
G1514.detail:
1. Be at peace with one another, without conflict: this is the absence of quarrels and divisions. In Romans 12:18, Paul urges Christians to "be at peace with all men," meaning not to enter into opposition, but to seek reconciliation as much as possible.
2. Maintain concord and harmony within a community: the verb implies action, an effort to preserve unity. In 1 Thessalonians 5:13, Paul says, "Be at peace among yourselves," inviting the community to keep harmony despite differences.
3. Cultivate inner and relational tranquility: this is the state of one who does not live in tension or fear. In 2 Corinthians 13:11, "live in peace" is part of a call to joy and perfection, a life of calm and serenity.
G1514.origine: The verb comes from εἰρήνη (eirênê), which means "peace." This Greek word often translates the Hebrew שׁלם (shalom) from the Old Testament, which expresses much more than an absence of war: it signifies wholeness, integrity, total well-being. Adding the verbal suffix (-euô) changes the noun into action: not "have peace" but "live in peace," "do the work of peace."
G1514.emploi: This verb appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul’s writings. In Mark 9:50, Jesus makes a succinct call: "be at peace with one another." Paul reiterates this teaching in his letters to the Romans (12:18), to the Corinthians (13:11), and to the Thessalonians (5:13), where he urges each community to cultivate peace not as a passive feeling, but as an active and vigilant attitude. The contexts show that this peace is threatened by conflicts, differences, and jealousies: this is why Paul must insistently command it. It is a command before being a gift.
G1514.portee: For the Christian, this verb is a call to personal and communal responsibility. Peace is not a grace that falls from heaven without effort: it is a disposition of heart and a daily practice that must be cultivated. It requires courage (to accept differences), gentleness (to refrain from imposing one’s will), and perseverance. By living in peace, the believer bears witness to the transformation of the Gospel and becomes an instrument of the God of love and peace.

sens: The absence of war and conflict between peoples or states
The absence of discord, agreement, and harmony among people
The state of security, calm, and well-being of one who fears nothing
The spiritual and inner peace that comes from a relationship with God through Christ
The blessing and favor of God
The action or person who soothes and reconciles
G1515.detail:
1. Public peace, the absence of war: this is the state of a country or people that is not fighting (Luke 14:32, where a king "asks for the conditions of peace" during war). The Church also lives in peace when it is not torn by persecution (Acts 9:31).

2. Peace among people is agreement, concord — the opposite of division. Jesus says he did not come to bring peace on earth, but "a sword": he forces everyone to choose sides, which divides families (Matthew 10:34). True peace arises from love, not from weakness (Romans 14:19).

3. Peace as a state of security and well-being: this is the calm of the heart of one who fears nothing. Jesus tells the disciples, "Go in peace" (Mark 5:34, Luke 7:50) — they can leave without fear. It is also a greeting formula (John 20:19: "Jesus said: Peace be with you").

4. The spiritual peace given by God through Christ: it reigns in the heart of the believer who has faith (Romans 5:1: "Being justified by faith, we have peace with God"). It is a "peace that surpasses all understanding" (Philippians 4:7).

5. Peace as divine blessing and favor: the expression "glory, honor, and peace" (Romans 2:10) lists the goods granted to one who does good — peace is the gift of God.

6. The one who soothes, who reconciles: Jesus is called "our peace" (Ephesians 2:14) because he has abolished the barrier between Jews and Gentiles and reconciled them into one body.
G1515.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes "passage" or "adjustment" — the idea of putting things in order. It translates the Hebrew שָׁלוֹם (shalom), a vast word that means complete well-being, wholeness, absence of rupture. Shalom is not simply the absence of war; it is a totality: health, prosperity, harmony with God and neighbor. The Septuagint (Greek version of the Old Testament) uses eirēnē to render this same word, thus uniting the two biblical cultures.
G1515.emploi: The word "peace" appears about 90 times in the New Testament, especially in the epistles. It is very common in apostolic greetings at the beginning of letters (Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:3, Ephesians 1:2, etc.): "Grace and peace to you." In the Gospels, Jesus often pronounces the wish "Go in peace" to those he has healed or sent (Mark 5:34, Luke 7:50). The Apostle Paul distinguishes peace with God (Romans 5:1) from the peace of God (Philippians 4:7). Peace is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), a virtue to actively pursue (Romans 14:19, Hebrews 12:14). Jesus promises his disciples a "peace that the world cannot give" (John 14:27), which contrasts with the false security of the world (1 Thessalonians 5:3). Peace is never merely tranquility for Paul, but a sign of reconciliation with God and harmony within the body of Christ.
G1515.portee: The word "peace" reminds us of the heart of Christian life: being at peace with God through the death and resurrection of Christ. This peace does not depend on circumstances — it can fill the believer's heart in the midst of tribulation. It is not inaction, but inner freedom to serve. It is also a responsibility: we are called to pursue and preserve it with all (Romans 14:19, Hebrews 12:14). Finally, true peace is the gift of God, not a human conquest — it is given to us in Jesus Christ, who is peace itself.

sens: That which calms, that produces peace
That is free from conflict and trouble
Characterizes one who seeks peace rather than strife
That proceeds from an attitude of gentleness and conciliation
G1516.detail:
1. The word "peaceful" describes that which calms and produces peace after a difficult period. In Hebrews 12:11, discipline, although painful at the moment, produces "a peaceful fruit of righteousness" for those who have been trained by it: it is a restored peace, a tranquility of conscience, and spiritual maturation.

2. It is also that which is free from conflicts, noise, or trouble. The wisdom from above in James 3:17 is described as "peaceable": it does not seek to impose its views by force or dispute, but acts in serenity.

3. The word characterizes one who, through their attitude, promotes harmony rather than disagreement. A peaceful person is someone who does not cultivate quarrels and prefers reconciliation.
G1516.origine: The word comes from "peace" (εἰρήνη, eirênê), which translates the Hebrew "shalom." It is an adjective naturally formed from this noun, just as "joyful" comes from "joy." The root evokes the idea of completeness, integrity, and absence of rupture — hence the transition from the physical sense of "peace" to the moral and spiritual sense of inner harmony and calm relationships.
G1516.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. It first describes the fruit of disciplinary chastisement in Hebrews 12:11: one who accepts correction produces a "peaceful justification," meaning spiritual growth marked by tranquility and assurance. In James 3:17, it characterizes divine wisdom itself: it is one of the primary qualities of true wisdom, which comes from above and opposes jealousy, ambition, and disorder. In both cases, the word denotes a state of controlled calm, the fruit of obedience or conformity to God's order.
G1516.portee: This word reminds us that true peace is not the absence of challenge or discipline, but the fruit of obedience and conformity to God. It is also a mark of true divine wisdom: a wisdom that does not seek to dominate or harm, but to reconcile and build up. For the believer, it is a call to seek and cultivate this peaceful peace, not through weakness, but through quiet strength and integrity.

sens: Establish peace, create harmony where there was tension or hostility
Reconcile, restore harmony between divided parties
In the biblical sense: reconcile humanity and the cosmos with God through the work of Christ
G1517.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to produce, to make peace": it is to create a situation of peace where there was previously discord or separation. The image is that of a craftsman who creates something. In Colossians 1:20, Christ "makes peace" by reconciling all of creation with God — it is His creative action that restores harmony.

2. More broadly, "make peace" means to reconcile two conflicting parties, to restore broken relationships. It is a voluntary and active act, not merely a cessation of hostilities, but a positive restoration of unity.

3. In the Pauline context, this verb carries a cosmic and spiritual significance: it is Christ who, through His sacrifice on the cross, accomplishes the ultimate reconciliation between sinful humanity and holy God, and restores divine order throughout all of creation.
G1517.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: εἰρήνη (eirēnē), "peace," and ποιέω (poieō), "to make, to produce, to create." This construction emphasizes the action of creating or producing peace, as one would fabricate an object. The word reflects the idea that peace is not a mere passive state, but the fruit of active work.
G1517.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Colossians 1:20, where Paul uses it to describe the reconciling work of Christ. In this passage, the apostle affirms that Christ "desired to reconcile all things to Himself" by "making peace through the blood of His cross." It is solemn language that expresses how the incarnation and death of Christ accomplish cosmic peace, reconciling heaven and earth, God and creation.
G1517.portee: This verb reminds Christians that peace with God is not earned by our efforts or merit, but is the completed work of Christ. It is an invitation to receive and live this peace already won by the cross. For the believer, this means that the deepest rifts — our separation from God — have been healed by the sacrifice of Christ.

sens: One who creates peace, who establishes agreement among men
One who works for reconciliation and harmony
One who acts to resolve conflicts and tensions
G1518.detail:
1. This word literally designates one who "makes" or "produces" peace. It is someone who does not merely remain neutral in the face of conflicts, but actively works to create agreement. In Matthew 5:9, Jesus blesses the peacemakers, promising that they will be called sons of God — an exceptional dignity.

2. The verb contained in this word means to create, to make, to produce: it is a peace that is made, constructed through work and personal commitment. It is not a passive or accidental peace, but the fruit of deliberate action.

3. This peace is not merely the absence of war or dispute, but the actual establishment of harmony, mutual understanding, and reconciliation between people or groups in conflict.
G1518.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "peace" (eirēnē) and "to make, to fabricate, to produce" (poieō). The root "to make" is the same that gives the word "poetry" in French — the idea of creation, of a productive action. This word appears only once in the New Testament, underscoring its particular importance in Jesus' teaching on true happiness.
G1518.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible: in Matthew 5:9, in the series of Beatitudes that Jesus pronounces in the Sermon on the Mount. It is a direct teaching on what God considers a blessed attitude. Jesus places the peacemaker among the greatest: he will be called "son of God," a title that reflects the divine character itself, since God is presented in the Bible as the source of all true peace.
G1518.portee: This passage invites the believer not to remain passive in the face of divisions and conflicts, but to become an active artisan of peace. It is a beatitude that values those who engage for reconciliation, sometimes at personal risk, rather than those who sidestep conflicts or take sides. For the Christian, it is a call to resemble God Himself, since only the one who brings peace will be called a son of God — a promise that shows that this work of peace touches the very heart of God.

sens: Movement of entry or approach to a place
Orientation of gaze or attention
Movement or progression to a limit point
Transformation or change of state
Duration or extension in time
Relation, connection, or destination of an action
G1519.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to enter a place or to approach it. "Jesus, having been born in Bethlehem of Judea… wise men from the East came to Jerusalem" (Matthew 2:1): they were heading toward the city, entering it. "They took him by the hand and led him to Damascus" (Acts 9:8): physical movement directed toward a destination.
2. To direct the gaze or mind in a direction. "Looking toward the heavens" (Matthew 6:26): the eyes turn upward. The image extends beyond physical sight to the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
3. To reach a limit, a threshold, an end. "We are going up to Jerusalem" (Luke 18:31): progression to a determined arrival point. This limit can be spatial or temporal.
4. To change or transform into something: to enter a new state. When one "turns anger into mercy" or when something "becomes" something else.
5. To extend or last over a period. "From generation to generation": time flows "toward" a continuous future. "Until this day", "until the end".
6. To express a relationship, a connection, an intention. "So that you may be deemed worthy of the kingdom" (2 Thessalonians 1:5): no physical movement, but a moral direction — toward what goal, for what purpose do we act? "To be good to someone": the relationship that connects two beings.
G1519.origine: The Greek εἰς (eis) comes from an Indo-European root expressing the idea of "in, into". Etymologically, it is related to other Greek prepositions that indicate direction or movement. In classical ancient Greek, it contrasts with other prepositions (ἐν "in", ἀπό "from"), but in New Testament Greek, it has become much more frequent and has taken on roles that classical Greek reserved for others. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew preposition בְ or אֶל ("to, into"), showing that the notion of movement or direction was central in Semitic thought as well.
G1519.emploi: εἰς is the most frequent preposition in the New Testament, with about 1,524 occurrences. It appears in every book and practically in every verse where movement or relationship is expressed. Its primary use is directional: with verbs of motion (to go, to come, to enter, to ascend), it marks the destination or arrival point — "to go to Jerusalem", "to enter a house". With verbs that do not indicate physical movement, it broadens its meaning: with verbs of vision, it indicates where one looks; with verbs of speech, to whom one speaks; with verbs of relationship, it expresses the connection or intention ("love toward someone"). It also serves to indicate the purpose or end of an action, the result of a change, or even duration. Its use has expanded so much in the late Greek of the New Testament that it often replaces the simple dative relationship. It is thus omnipresent and has great semantic flexibility.
G1519.portee: This preposition invites the reader to see the Christian life as an oriented movement. Believers do not stagnate; they "go toward" a destination — toward Jesus, toward the kingdom, toward holiness. It emphasizes that every action, every decision, every feeling has a direction and an end. Understanding εἰς helps to grasp that faith is not a static position but an orientation of the whole being toward God and His purpose. It also shows how the most ordinary gestures and words (to look, to speak, to go) are never neutral: they are always directed toward someone or something.

sens: An object or person, to the exclusion of others
Which is unique, unparalleled, to which no other can be compared
Each taken individually from a group
In a particular or special manner
In the ordinal sense, first
G1520.detail:
1. The most common meaning: there is only one thing or one person, not two or more. For example, in Matthew 5:18, Jesus says that not a single iota will disappear from the law. This is the simple meaning of the number one.
2. When one wants to emphasize absolute uniqueness, the incomparable nature: only God can forgive sins (Mark 2:7). There is only one shepherd, one flock (John 10:16). Here, "only" firmly excludes any alternative.
3. Distributed among several: each receives a talent, one this, another that (Matthew 25:15). This is the sense where individuals are enumerated from a group.
4. In union or concord, particularly in theological expressions: one God and Father of all (Ephesians 4:6), one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:9). The word emphasizes unity and indivisibility.
5. Very rarely, it takes the ordinal sense of "first" (Matthew 28:1, the first day of the week), a usage borrowed from Hebrew.
G1520.origine: The Greek word εἷς comes from a very ancient root meaning "one". It is the fundamental word for expressing numerical unity. It corresponds to the Hebrew אֶחָד (echad), which already had the same nuances: a number, uniqueness, unity. The Greek translators of the Old Testament regularly rendered this Hebrew word with the Greek εἷς, which explains why all the meanings of the Hebrew word are found in Greek.
G1520.emploi: The word appears more than 297 times in the New Testament, making it an extremely frequent word. It is used everywhere: for simple counting (one, two, three), to express divine uniqueness ("one God"), for the unity of the Church or the Spirit, and to individually enumerate the members of a community. In the Pauline letters, it often has a marked theological significance, expressing the unity of the body of Christ. In the Gospels, it can be very ordinary (a man, a woman) or very meaningful (one commandment, one Father). Jesus uses it to emphasize the absolute: one Master, one law.
G1520.portee: This word teaches the believer two essential things: on one hand, the singularity and incomparability of God and His law, which do not allow for sharing or dilution; on the other hand, the deep unity of the people of God and His Spirit, despite the diversity of gifts and calls. Meditating on these uses strengthens faith in divine uniqueness and in the uniqueness of the body of Christ.

sens: To bring someone or something into a place
To bring someone to someone or before someone
To lead someone to a specific location
To bring something by leading it with oneself
G1521.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to pass the threshold of a place, to introduce. When the servant girl "introduces" Peter to the high priest (John 18:16), she leads him inside. This is the most concrete image of the word.

2. More broadly, it means to bring someone to present them or put them in the presence of someone else. The parents "bring" the child Jesus to the temple (Luke 2:27): they lead him there to offer him to the Lord according to the Law.

3. The word is also used to lead someone from one point to another, especially to a place of authority or judgment. Jesus is "led" to the house of the high priest (Luke 22:54) and Saul is "led" to Damascus (Acts 9:8).

4. In a broader sense, it means to bring or lead people for a specific purpose. The servant must "bring" the poor and the lame to the feast (Luke 14:21): he leads them so they can join in.
G1521.origine: The word is composed of εἰς ("into", "in") and ἄγω ("to lead", "to bring"). The basic image is therefore to lead someone into a place or into someone's presence. In Hebrew, it commonly translates בּוֹא in the causative form ("to bring in"), which carries the same idea of crossing a threshold or accessing a space.
G1521.emploi: The verb εἰσάγω appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospel of Luke and Acts. It describes very concrete actions: bringing someone to a place, presenting them before authorities, or leading them to a specific location. In Luke, it is a simple narrative movement verb. In Acts, it retains this sense of leading someone (notably Saul to Damascus, Jesus before the authorities), but also of introducing a people into a land (Acts 7:45: Joshua "introduces" the fathers into Canaan). In Hebrews 1:6, it takes on a more solemn tone: introducing the Son into the world or the universe. The context changes, but the idea of leading inward, presenting, or bringing in remains constant.
G1521.portee: This verb speaks of movement, the passage from one state or place to another. For the believer, it reminds us that we are often "brought" before God or led by His providence—like Saul on the road to Damascus. It is a word of action and obedience: we do not remain passive; we are led, guided, introduced into God's plan. It invites us to recognize how God leads us and presents us before Him, just as the parents presented Jesus at the temple.

sens: To listen favorably to a prayer or request
To obey a word, an order
To accept, to give one's assent
G1522.detail:
1. To grant means that God listens and responds favorably to someone's prayer. This is the most common meaning in the New Testament: when we pray, we hope to be granted, meaning that God hears and acts. In Luke 1:13, the angel announces to Zechariah: "Your prayer has been granted," which means that God has heard and will give what he asked for (a son). Similarly, in Acts 10:31, God tells Cornelius that his prayer has been granted and that his alms are not forgotten.
2. To grant can also mean to obey or submit to an order or a word. In 1 Corinthians 14:21, Paul cites the Law: "It is through men of another tongue that I will speak to this people, and they will not listen to me"—here, "not listen to me" means to refuse to obey, to submit to God's word.
3. In an active usage, to grant also refers to one who accepts, who gives their agreement. The idea is always one of hearing favorably and responding positively.
G1522.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and combines the idea of "entering into" (the preposition eis-) with "to listen" (akouō). It literally means "to listen while taking into consideration," or "to listen and act." In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew word "shamac" (שָׁמַע), which means both to listen and to obey: in biblical Hebrew, listening to God is already to obey Him. The word conveys this dual idea: to listen is to hear, but it is also, in the heart, to accept and execute.
G1522.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the uses of the Segond that we know. It is first used for prayer: God grants the prayer (Luke 1:13, Acts 10:31, Hebrews 5:7), or one wonders if they will be granted (Matthew 6:7). It is also used for obedience: to not grant someone means to refuse to listen to them, that is, to disobey (1 Corinthians 14:21). The context shows that it is always a matter of personal relationship: someone addresses someone else (in prayer or in order), and to be granted is to receive a favorable response.
G1522.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that prayer is not a solitary monologue: it is addressed to a God who listens and can respond. To be granted does not mean to automatically obtain what we ask for, but to know that God hears us and takes our request seriously. It also invites us to truly "listen" to God in return, that is, to obey Him, for to grant also means to accept His word.

sens: To receive someone or something in one's presence, to admit them
To accept a person into one's community or covenant
G1523.detail:
1. To welcome means to receive someone or something, to admit them into a place or to oneself. It is the idea of saying "yes" to a presence, of creating a place for it. In 2 Corinthians 6:17, God promises: "I will welcome you"—He prepares to receive those who separate from impurity, like a father who opens his house to his children returning to him.
2. More broadly, to welcome means to integrate someone into a covenant or relationship. God welcomes those who respond to His call by purifying themselves: this is not a mere social welcome, but an acceptance into the family of God, a return to communion with Him.
G1523.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: "eis" (into, in) and "dechomai" (to receive, to welcome). The starting image is that of bringing something or someone inside—to receive them, to take them with oneself. In Greek, "dechomai" is a classical verb for benevolent welcome. When Paul uses it, he plays on this idea: God brings us into Himself, completely receives us.
G1523.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 6:17. Paul cites here a passage from the Old Testament (Isaiah 52:11) to exhort the Corinthians to separate from what is impure and defiled. God then promises to welcome them—this is a word of grace and restoration. The context shows that God's welcome depends on our willingness to turn away from impurity: it is a conditional promise, but also an assurance that God does not reject anyone who returns to Him.
G1523.portee: This word reminds us of a fundamental truth: God welcomes. There is no closed door for one who repents and separates from evil. This promise of welcome calms the fear of rejection and strengthens the certainty that anyone who abandons impurity to draw near to God will be received with kindness. It is an invitation to purity coupled with the assurance that God honors those who respond to His call.

sens: To cross the threshold of a place, to go in to be inside
To present oneself to someone
To perform an action or a religious act by entering a sacred space
G1524.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is to cross a door or threshold to be inside a place: it is the simple action of going inside. Peter and John are going to enter the temple to pray, and the beggar sees them preparing to do so (Acts 3:3). It is the physical movement from outside to inside.

2. The word can also mean to present oneself, to come to someone. When Paul goes to see James, it is said that he enters to see him, meaning he goes to his home or the place where James is (Acts 21:18).

3. In a religious context, entering takes on a particular significance: it is to perform an action or fulfill a function by entering a consecrated space. The priests enter the tabernacle to perform worship; Paul enters the temple to carry out the purification rites (Acts 21:26 and Hebrews 9:6). To enter then truly means to enter to act.
G1524.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: εἰς (eis), which means "to, into," and ἔρχομαι (erchomai), which means "to go, to come." Together, they form the idea of going inside. In Hebrew, it is the verb בּוֹא (bo'a) that expresses the same movement: to come, to go, to enter. This Hebrew verb is found both in the simple physical sense (crossing a door) and in the figurative or ritual sense (entering into a relationship with God or entering into possession of a promise).
G1524.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the New Testament, only in the Acts of the Apostles and the Epistle to the Hebrews. In Acts, it often refers to the moment when someone crosses the threshold of the temple or presents themselves to a person: Peter and John enter the temple to pray, Paul enters to perform a purification rite, and he enters to see James. In Hebrews 9:6, we find the ritual use: the priests enter the tabernacle to perform their service. The context is always concrete — it is truly a physical movement — but often related to important or sacred moments in the life of the early Church.
G1524.portee: This word reminds us that our acts of faith are not internal or abstract, but unfold in the real world, in places and with people. When Peter and John enter the temple, or when Paul enters to purify himself, it is the concrete commitment of the body and life. For the Christian, this speaks to the importance of crossing thresholds: that of prayer in community, that of confessing one's faith to others, that of entering into the space of worship. It is an invitation not just to believe from afar, but to present oneself, to move forward, to act.

sens: To physically penetrate a place, a house, a building
To access a space or cross a threshold (door, mountain, etc.)
To intrude or slip into a place (referring to bad influences)
To occur, to happen, to arrive (referring to a feeling or inner reality)
To access a spiritual state or condition (the Kingdom, eternal life, rest)
G1525.detail:
1. The most direct meaning: to physically penetrate a closed or defined place. "Jesus entered the house" (Matthew 9:25), "Wherever he enters, say to the master of the house" (Mark 14:14). It is the simple action of crossing a door or threshold.
2. To access a space by passing through a path or point of entry. "I will show you the way that leads to eternal life" contrasts with "enter through the narrow gate" (Matthew 7:13), where it is indeed crossing the threshold.
3. To intrude secretly or harmfully: when an evil spirit "entered" someone (Luke 8:30), or when Satan "entered" Judas (John 13:27), the image is that of an intrusion that takes possession.
4. To occur or happen in an inner way: "Do not lead us into temptation" (Matthew 26:41, where the verb literally means "to enter into"). Thoughts "enter" into the heart (Luke 9:46).
5. To access a major spiritual condition or state: "to enter the Kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 5:20, 7:21), "to enter into life" (Matthew 18:8, 19:17), "to enter into rest" (Hebrews 3:11). It is to attain or possess a reality of salvation and communion with God.
G1525.origine: The word comes from the prefix εἰς (into, toward) combined with ἔρχομαι (to come, to go). This root ἔρχομαι expresses simple movement, and the prefix specifies the direction: to enter is "to come into." In Hebrew, we mainly find בּוֹא (bô'a, to come, to enter), which shares the same idea of directed movement. It is a very ancient word in the vocabulary of movement and access.
G1525.emploi: The verb appears 184 times in the New Testament, more than half in Matthew and Luke. Concrete uses dominate: Jesus enters synagogues, houses, the temple. But very quickly, figurative meanings appear, particularly in Jesus' teachings. Matthew accumulates expressions like "enter the Kingdom," "enter into life," "enter into the joy of the Lord," modeled on Aramaic formulas from Judaism to describe access to the final condition of the elect. The Acts and the Epistle to the Hebrews also use the verb in a very spiritual way: entering into the rest of God (Hebrews 3-4), or, negatively, entering into temptation. It is therefore a word that naturally glides from the physical to the spiritual, which makes its richness in preaching.
G1525.portee: This word reminds us that faith is not an abstract theory, but a real entry into a new relationship and condition. When Jesus says, "No one can enter the Kingdom unless he is born again" (John 3), he evokes a crossing, a boundary to pass, a transformation that allows us to access another reality. For the Christian, "to enter" also means to guard against what seeks to contaminate us (the evil spirit, temptation) and to seek to penetrate into intimacy with God, just as one enters a house to live there.

sens: To invite someone to enter a place
To welcome by offering hospitality
G1528.detail:
1. The word denotes the action of inviting someone to cross a door, to enter a closed space. In Acts 10:23, Peter "brought in" the messengers sent by Cornelius: he invited them to cross the threshold of his house in Joppa, physically welcoming them.
2. Beyond the simple gesture, "to bring in" implies hospitality, a kind welcome. Peter does not just open the door for them; he "lodged them," meaning he received them as guests, offering them a place of rest.
G1528.origine: The word combines two elements: "eis" (inside, into) and "kaleo" (to call, to invite). The basic image is therefore to call someone to enter. It is a relatively uncommon compound word in the Greek of the New Testament, formed simply and directly to express physical welcome.
G1528.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:23. In this crucial passage, Peter welcomes the three messengers sent by Cornelius, a Roman officer seeking to know the message of Christ. This gesture of hospitality is significant: it shows Peter overcoming his prejudices and welcoming Gentiles, which signals the great turning point of the nascent Church towards non-Jews.
G1528.portee: This simple gesture of bringing in and lodging illustrates how the Christian faith manifests concretely: through the welcome of the stranger, unguarded hospitality, and the opening of heart and home. It is a lesson on practical love and welcoming one's neighbor, two central values of the Gospel.

sens: action d'entrer ou de venir quelque part
lieu ou moyen par lequel on entre
accès à un endroit, surtout sacré
arrivée d'une personne
G1529.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: the action of crossing a threshold, going from outside to inside. In Acts 13:24, it refers to the "coming" of Jesus, His arrival in the world — the very act of entering the scene. In 1 Thessalonians 2:1, the "arrival" of Paul among the Thessalonians denotes the moment he presented himself to them.
2. The place or way by which one enters somewhere: a door, a passage. In Hebrews 10:19, the "entry" into the sanctuary is primarily the physical path, the concrete possibility of crossing the veil of the temple.
3. Access in the sense of permission, the right to approach — especially before God or an authority. In 1 Thessalonians 1:9, the "access" that the apostles had with the Thessalonians speaks of the reception they were granted, the freedom they had to approach.
4. In a spiritual and theological sense: access to salvation, to the presence of God. In 2 Peter 1:11, the "entry" into the eternal kingdom is the gift of being able to enter, at the time of the final judgment, into the definitive dwelling with Christ.
G1529.origine: The word comes from two combined Greek roots: εἰς (eis, "into") and ὁδός (hodos, "way, path"). The starting image is therefore literally "way to the inside" or "entry path." In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), this word often translates the Hebrew בּוֹא (bô', "to enter, to come"). The family of the Greek word also includes the verb εἴσειμι ("to enter"). It is a word that blends the idea of movement (going) and that of crossing a boundary (passing inside).
G1529.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, concentrated in the Pauline epistles and the Epistle to the Hebrews. In Acts 13:24, it denotes the historical arrival of Jesus. In 1 Thessalonians 1:9 and 2:1, it describes the arrival and reception of the apostles — its meaning follows the common Pauline usage to speak of someone's coming to a city or mission. In Hebrews 10:19, the word shifts from the physical to the spiritual: the entry becomes a liturgical and spiritual access to the Holy of Holies, made possible by the sacrifice of Christ. In 2 Peter 1:11, it takes on its most eschatological meaning: the entry into the eternal kingdom, the final access to the glory of God. The word can therefore denote both a concrete arrival and a privilege or right of access.
G1529.portee: This word reminds the reader that access to God is not a right but a gift. By the blood of Jesus, the closed path of the temple is opened: believers now have an "entry" into the divine presence, once reserved for the high priest alone. It also speaks of hope: our final entry into the eternal kingdom is assured if we remain faithful. It is a word of invitation and restored freedom.

sens: Se précipiter dans un lieu avec urgence et impulsivité
Faire irruption soudainement
G1530.detail:
1. The verb depicts the action of someone who enters abruptly somewhere, driven by a strong emotion or urgent necessity. It is a quick and involuntary movement. In Acts 16:29, the jailer of Philippi, abruptly awakened by an earthquake that opened the prison doors, rushes into the cell where Paul and Silas are confined: he fears the worst and wants to immediately check on the state of the prisoners.
2. The word emphasizes the emotional impulse that drives one to act without thinking: fear, curiosity, or physical urgency. This hasty action without calculation reveals the inner state of the one who acts.
G1530.origine: The verb is composed of two elements: the prefix *eis* ("into") and *pēdaō* ("to rush in," "to leap"), which evokes the rapid movement of an animal that leaps forward. The root *pēd-* suggests the idea of jumping or leaping forcefully. In Hebrew, the Old Testament Greek sometimes translates sudden entry into a place with this verb (as in Amos 5:19 where the Hebrew word literally means "to come").
G1530.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 16:29, where it describes the behavior of the jailer of Philippi at the moment of the earthquake. The use of the word emphasizes the spontaneity and urgency of his gesture: he does not deliberate, he acts. This impulsive action contrasts sharply with what follows: trembling, he falls at Paul’s feet and asks how to be saved. The verb thus prepares the reader to understand that a strong emotion has opened the jailer to the question of salvation.
G1530.portee: This small word reveals how divine providence can touch a heart through dramatic circumstances. The jailer's urgency shows that the earthquake was not just a physical catastrophe, but a signal that shattered his certainties and pushed him to seek the truth. For the Christian, this reminds us that God can use unexpected events to bring us back to Him.

sens: Se mouvoir pour aller à l'intérieur d'un lieu
Franchir le seuil d'une maison, d'un bâtiment
Se diriger vers un endroit précis
Pénétrer physiquement (en parlant d'objets ou d'aliments)
Avoir accès à un état ou une condition spirituelle
S'associer avec quelqu'un, fréquenter
G1531.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to move toward the inside of a closed or defined space. One "enters" somewhere: into a house (Mark 5:40, where Jesus enters the room of the sick child), into a synagogue (Mark 1:21), into the city (Luke 19:30).

2. When speaking of objects or food, the verb describes how they physically penetrate the body. "What goes into the mouth goes into the stomach" (Matthew 15:17): the food crosses the barrier of the lips and enters the digestive tract.

3. Spiritually, the verb expresses access to a divine reality: "How hard it is for those who have riches to enter the kingdom of God!" (Luke 18:24). Here, "enter" means to access, to be admitted, to participate.

4. The verb can also mean "to associate with," "to frequent someone": after the resurrection, Paul "entered and exited" with the apostles (Acts 9:28), meaning he was with them, in communion with them.
G1531.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "eis" (into, inside) and the verb "poreuō" (to walk, to go, to direct oneself). This combination creates the meaning of "going inside," "penetrating." In Hebrew, the corresponding verb in the Greek Old Testament is primarily "bôʾ" (בּוֹא), which carries the same idea of crossing an entry, moving toward the inside. The family of the word includes related verbs like "eiserchomai" (to enter through a door) and the noun "poreia" (way, journey).
G1531.emploi: This verb appears 18 times in the New Testament, mainly in the four Gospels and Acts. Mark and Luke use it primarily to describe the entries of Jesus and His disciples into places: synagogues, cities, houses. The verb also applies to physical realities (food, thoughts that penetrate the heart) and spiritual ones (access to the kingdom of God). In Acts 8:3, Paul "enters from house to house" to persecute believers; in Acts 9:28, he "enters and exits" with the apostles after his conversion. The meaning becomes clearer depending on the context: concrete movement toward a place, or moral and spiritual penetration.
G1531.portee: This verb invites the reader to reflect on what "enters" their spiritual life: not only thoughts and desires (Mark 4:19), but also the Word, faith, and ultimately access to the kingdom of God. It reminds us that physical barriers mean nothing before the heavenly kingdom — what matters is the inner access, the spiritual admission that only grace offers.

sens: to run in
to rush eagerly
G1532.detail:
1. To run while entering somewhere, to hurry from one place to another: the servant girl Rhoda, after recognizing Peter's voice at the door of the house, "ran" to announce to the others that Peter was outside (Acts 12:14). The movement is quick and the intention clear: she moves rapidly from one place to another to convey news.
2. To rush eagerly, to hurry towards someone or something: the verb emphasizes the joyful haste and urgency of the person running, driven by emotion or the desire to act quickly. For Rhoda, it is the joy of recognizing Peter that propels her swift action.
G1532.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "eis" (into) and "trechō" (to run). This combination creates the idea of running inward, to enter running. The root "trechō" is common in the New Testament to express rapid movement, effort, or running, whether physical or figurative. The preposition "eis" specifies the direction: it is always to run *toward* or *into* something.
G1532.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 12:14. It describes the moment when Rhoda, the servant of Mary the mother of John, recognizes Peter's voice at the door and, instead of opening, immediately runs inside to announce to the others that Peter has arrived. The action is simple but revealing: it shows the joyful eagerness of this young girl in the face of extraordinary news. It is a vivid, concrete word that paints a scene of primitive Church life.
G1532.portee: This small verb reminds us that the most ordinary gestures—running, opening a door, announcing news—can be filled with joy and urgency when God acts. Rhoda's haste reflects the liveliness with which the disciples welcomed Peter's return after his miraculous deliverance from prison. It is a human detail that humanizes the biblical narrative and shows how faith is lived in the small movements of daily life.

sens: To physically bring someone or something into a place
To bring someone before an authority or a judge
To lead the mind toward a thought, a temptation, a behavior
To convey to someone (information, a word)
G1533.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to bring in. Luke reports that men sought to "bring in" a paralytic to Jesus (Luke 5:18), and since they could not, they "let him down" through the roof (Luke 5:19). It is the physical movement of bringing someone or something from one place to another.
2. To bring someone before a court or authority to be judged. Jesus warns his disciples: "When you are brought before synagogues, rulers, and authorities" (Luke 12:11), meaning they will be dragged before these official bodies to be questioned.
3. To gradually lead the mind or will toward something—here, toward sin or wrongdoing. In the Lord's Prayer, Jesus says: "And lead us not into temptation" (Matthew 6:13, Luke 11:4), meaning do not push us, do not lead us to fall into sin.
4. To convey or make a word, a thought heard. The Athenians say to Paul: "You bring strange things to our ears" (Acts 17:20), his words reach their ears and strike their minds.
G1533.origine: The word is composed of "eis" (into) and "phero" (to carry, to bring). The basic image is therefore "to carry inward," "to bring in." In Hebrew, the corresponding verb often translated by this Greek word is the intensive form of "bôa'" (to enter), which reinforces the idea of actively bringing in. This simple composition—entering + voluntary action—accounts for all the uses, from the most physical to the most moral.
G1533.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke. It first denotes the material action of bringing someone somewhere (Luke 5:18-19), then expands to the idea of leading before a tribunal (Luke 12:11), making a word heard (Acts 17:20), or leading the mind toward evil (Matthew 6:13, Luke 11:4). Hebrews 13:11 uses it for the bodies of victims "brought" outside the camp. The word does not carry moral ambiguity in itself: it all depends on what is being brought in or where one is being led.
G1533.portee: For the believer, this word sheds light on two important aspects. First, it shows that temptation to sin is an external power that seeks to "lead" us toward evil—God never pushes us there. By praying "lead us not into temptation," we acknowledge that our strength is fragile and we ask God to keep us from paths that would lead us away from Him. Secondly, the verb reminds us that the Word of God "brings us in" to His presence and truth: it leads us from the outside (ignorance) to the inside (communion with God).

sens: Marks succession in time: what comes after something else
Introduces a list: first, second, third...
Marks a consequence or conclusion in reasoning
G1534.detail:
1. This is the most common meaning: one event follows another in time. For example, in John 19:27, Jesus speaks to his mother, then he speaks to the disciple—two actions that succeed each other. Similarly, in Mark 4:17, persecution comes first, then it causes the fall. This word depicts the passage of time, step by step.

2. In an enumeration or list, εἶτα separates elements to mentally number them. In 1 Corinthians 15:5, Paul recounts: Christ appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve, then to more than five hundred brothers—he thus enumerates the successive appearances of the resurrection.

3. In an argument or reasoning, this word can mean "therefore" or "as a result." It is less a succession of facts than a transition in thought: from a premise, one moves to the conclusion that follows.
G1534.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and expresses temporal or logical order. It belongs to the family of succession adverbs, such as καὶ τότε ("and then"). Its fundamental meaning is "what follows," marking a progression from one moment or idea to the next.
G1534.emploi: The word εἶτα appears 14 times in the New Testament. It is used mainly to mark temporal succession: in Mark 8:25, Jesus heals a blind man and then he sees; in Luke 8:12, the word is sown, then the devil takes it away. Paul also uses it to enumerate (the appearances of the risen Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:5-7), and to chain the steps of a moral progression (in James 1:15, desire conceives, then it gives birth to sin). In 1 Timothy 3:10, deacons are tested first, then they serve—two distinct phases. The word thus articulates the unfolding of biblical events.
G1534.portee: This small word helps the reader follow the course of events and the logic of thought. By showing how one thing follows another, it reveals the progression of God's plan and the cause-effect relationship in the history of salvation. It invites the believer to see that in the Christian life as well, steps follow one another: first faith, then discipleship, then maturity—everything has its time.

sens: conjunction that enumerates two or more possibilities or categories without preference or exclusion
marks indifference between the terms: it does not matter which one
G1535.detail:
1. This double conjunction enumerates distinct cases or situations, placing them on the same level. It connects alternatives without favoring any. In 1 Corinthians 8:5, Paul enumerates: "if there are beings called gods, either in heaven or on earth" — he describes all categories of deities that the pagans recognize, without privileging any.
2. The enumeration often expresses the speaker's indifference: it does not matter which of the two (or several) options occurs. In Philippians 1:18, Paul says, "whether for appearance or sincerely, Christ is proclaimed no less" — he asserts that the outcome (the proclamation of Christ) is valid in all cases.
G1535.origine: Εἴτε (eite) comes from the Greek εἰ (ei, "if"), the fundamental conditional conjunction, to which the suffix -τε (-te), an ancient distributive morpheme, is added. This formation expresses the idea of "one or the other" without distinction. It commonly appears in classical Greek literature to enumerate without hierarchy.
G1535.emploi: Εἴτε appears 29 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul's epistles (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philippians, etc.). It almost always appears in pairs (εἴτε...εἴτε) to enumerate two or three terms. In Romans 12:6-8, Paul enumerates the spiritual gifts: "either [the gift] of prophecy... or [the gift] of service..." without order of importance. It also expresses indifference or neutrality regarding variations: in 1 Corinthians 13:8, "prophecies will cease, tongues will cease" enumerates cessations without distinction. The enumeration can refer to places (Colossians 1:16: "either thrones or dominions"), states (living or dead), or modalities (sincerity or appearance).
G1535.portee: This small conjunction teaches useful wisdom: in the face of various realities or modalities that we do not control, what matters is the essential. Paul uses it to serve the message of salvation: regardless of the context or category, what is important is that Christ is proclaimed or that grace is recognized. It invites the reader to see beyond the surface.

sens: to go out, come from a place, escape from
to originate from, to be derived from (birth, origin)
to come from, to emanate from (source, author, cause)
to be composed of, to be made of (material, substance)
to distinguish, to be drawn from (among a group)
from, since a moment or point
G1537.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: "ἐκ" marks a movement of exit or separation from a place or situation. One goes "out of" the house, escapes "from" prison, rises "from" the table. Example: "When they went out" (Acts 13:42) translates a verb whose object is introduced by ἐκ.
2. When speaking of birth or genealogy, ἐκ indicates that a person is "derived from" their parents or lineage. Example: "Judah begot from Tamar" (Matthew 1:3) — Tamar is the mother, and Judah begets children who come from her.
3. Ἐκ marks the origin or source from which a word, action, or feeling comes: a word "comes from" God, an act "emanates from" the heart, a thought "originates from" faith. Example: "This circumcision does not come from Moses, for it comes from the patriarchs" (John 7:22).
4. When describing the material or substance of which something is made, ἐκ functions like "in," "of." A crown "of" thorns, a whip "of" cords: we understand what "composes" the object.
5. Among a group, a person is "drawn from," "distinguished from" the multitude: a leper "among" ten, or a person "among" the priests of a given class. Example: "a priest... of the class of Abijah" (Luke 1:5).
6. In terms of time, ἐκ marks the starting point: "since" one was born, "from" that moment. This is less common but the meaning remains: one begins "from" a given instant.
G1537.origine: Ἐκ is a very ancient preposition in Greek, identical to the Latin "ex." It fundamentally expresses the idea of "coming out of," "coming from," "starting from." In classical Greek, it is used before a consonant and ἐξ before a vowel (an alternation phenomenon that has traces in French: "ex" becomes "é" in Old French). The corresponding Hebrew word is often מִן ("min"), which also means "from," "out of." This preposition evokes the image of separation or extraction: something that was "inside" goes "outside."
G1537.emploi: Ἐκ is the most frequently used preposition in the New Testament (767 occurrences according to the data). It appears massively in the Gospel of Matthew, in the Gospel of John, and in Acts. It serves to express four main domains: (1) spatial movement (leaving a place, going out of), (2) genealogical or physical origin (being born of, descending from), (3) the source of an action or quality (coming from God, emanating from the heart), (4) the material or composition (made of, woven of). In certain passages, especially in John, ἐκ takes on a strong theological significance: "Whoever is born of God" (1 John 3:9) expresses belonging to God, a spiritual filiation. Its frequency and range of use make it a fundamental preposition for understanding biblical thought: it constantly connects the object or action to its source or starting point.
G1537.portee: For the Christian reader, ἐκ invites an awareness of the link between who we are and where we come from. When Scripture says that one is "born of God" or that "it is from the abundance of the heart that the mouth speaks," it reminds us that our actions, our words, our thoughts reveal our source. This engages a responsibility: where does what I have in my heart come from? It also opens up a hope: if I am born of God, my deep nature is transformed. This preposition, seemingly grammatical, thus structures a theology of origin and filiation that runs throughout the New Testament.

sens: each person taken individually
each thing taken one after another
each one separately, individually
G1538.detail:
1. The word designates each person or each thing considered individually, mentally separating the group into units. It conveys the idea that no one is forgotten, that everyone is counted one by one: "the Son of Man will repay each according to his works" (Matthew 16:27) means that each individual will receive their personal reward, no one will escape God's judgment.
2. Used in the plural, the word can also express the whole formed by all individuals: "each of them received the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38) shows that none were forgotten in the divine gift.
3. The expression "each according to his measure" (as in 1 Corinthians 12:11 where each receives their gifts) emphasizes that diverse realities are personally distributed to each believer: God does not treat everyone identically, but respects the uniqueness of each.
G1538.origine: The word comes from a very ancient Greek root expressing distinction and separation. It was used in classical Greek (by Homer and Greek historians) to enumerate the elements of a set by taking them one by one. It is fundamentally a distributive word: it distributes an action or quality to each unit of a group, rather than treating them globally.
G1538.emploi: The word appears 77 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul's epistles and the Gospels. Paul constantly uses it to remind that each believer has personal responsibility, a unique part, particular gifts: in teachings about the Church, he emphasizes that "each received the gift of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 2:38) or that "each has received from God his own measure" (1 Corinthians 12:7, 11). In Luke, it appears in contexts of counting or distribution ("each village" in Luke 2:3; "each healed person"). Revelation uses it to show that the final judgment reaches each human individually.
G1538.portee: This word reminds the Christian that they are never lost in the crowd in God's eyes: each receives personal attention, each must account for their actions. It also invites not to envy the neighbor's share, but to humbly accept the gift that God has given to each. It is a word of dignity and responsibility for the believer.

sens: every time, without exception
constantly and repeatedly
without interruption, continuously
G1539.detail:
1. Every time: the word refers to what occurs or is done on every occasion, without exception — like when Peter wants to ensure that believers remember his teachings at every reminder (2 Peter 1:15, "I will make every effort to see that after my departure you will always be able to remember these things").
2. Constantly: the idea is one of habitual and reliable repetition, something that recurs regularly over time, without forgetfulness or slackening.
3. Continuously: by extension, this expresses permanence, a constant presence of memory or action in the mind and life.
G1539.origine: The Greek word ἑκάστοτε is composed of ἑκάστος ("each, every") and a repetitive element (-ότε) that reinforces the idea of repetition. It conveys the habit, action, or state that recurs regularly. The word family includes ἑκάστῳ ("to each") and ἑκάστου ("of each"), all expressing the idea of totality and succession.
G1539.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:15, where the apostle Peter asserts that his readers will be able to "always" remember the teaching he conveys to them in writing. It is a temporal adverb that emphasizes continuity and reliability: thanks to this letter, the memory of his words will remain constantly accessible and alive in the Church.
