G1539.portee: This word reminds us that the Word of God, transmitted and meditated upon, becomes a lasting presence in the life of the believer. It is not a fleeting illumination, but a resource to which one continually returns, nourishing faith and memory at every moment of the Christian life.

sens: The number 100, ten times ten
Large quantity, numerous or abundant
Generous yield or production
Gathering or grouping of many people
G1540.detail:
1. "Hundred" is the number 100 itself, used simply for counting or measuring: a defined quantity of things. John 19:39 mentions "a hundred pounds" of myrrh and aloes brought for the burial of Jesus — a precise measured quantity.

2. The number hundred also represents abundance, fullness, what is rich and generous. When a grain of wheat "bears fruit, a hundredfold" (Matthew 13:8), it is not just a calculation: it is the image of an extraordinary blessing, a harvest that exceeds normal expectation.

3. In Jesus' parables, hundred symbolizes the completeness and perfection of a result: a harvest of "a hundred" means fruit brought to its maximum fulfillment (Mark 4:8, 20).

4. Hundred can also refer to an organized group or a large assembly: "seated in groups of hundreds and fifties" (Mark 6:40), or "one hundred forty-four thousand" in John's vision (Revelation 14:1), suggesting an innumerable and organized people.
G1540.origine: The Greek word ἑκατόν comes from an ancient Indo-European root and literally means "hundred." It is a fundamental cardinal number, very stable in ancient languages. It regularly translates the Hebrew מְאָה (meah) in the Greek Old Testament. The word does not have a rich family of biblical derivatives: it is simply used to denote this number in all situations where the Bible needs it.
G1540.emploi: The word "hundred" appears 17 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. It is used first for precise counts: a hundred sheep (Matthew 18:12), a hundred measures of oil (Luke 16:6), a hundred pounds of myrrh (John 19:39). It also appears in the parables of the Kingdom: the seed that bears "a hundredfold" is a key theme in Matthew 13 and Mark 4, where the number emphasizes extraordinary blessing. In Revelation, "one hundred forty-four thousand" (Revelation 14:1) and "a hundred cubits" (Revelation 21:17) express symbolic quantities related to the heavenly city and the people of God. Finally, Mark 6:40 uses it to organize a crowd: the disciples have the people sit "in groups of hundreds and fifties," showing how a large number can be orderly.
G1540.portee: The number hundred in the Bible always evokes abundance and divine blessing. For the disciple, the promise that the seed bears "a hundredfold" speaks of supernatural fruitfulness: when one gives to the Kingdom, God multiplies the fruit far beyond what one dares to hope. The parable of the hundred sheep also shows that each one matters in God's eyes — even if He has a thousand, He does not cease to seek the one that has gone astray. These images help the believer understand that God thinks in terms of fullness and abundance, not of petty calculations.

sens: who is one hundred years old
of extremely advanced age
G1541.detail:
1. This word literally refers to someone who has reached the age of one hundred years. It is the age at which Abraham was when the promised child, Isaac, was to be born (Romans 4:19). This exceptional age underscores the natural impossibility of the promised birth.
2. Broadly, it expresses an age so advanced that it is a miracle if life continues and if a new birth can occur. In Abraham's case, this extreme age contrasts with the divine promise, highlighting that only faith can conceive what is humanly impossible (Romans 4:19).
G1541.origine: The word is composed of two Greek terms: "hekatón" (hundred) and "etês" (year). It translates the Hebrew expression "ben meah shana" (literally "son of a hundred years"), a Hebrew phrase used to designate someone who is one hundred years old. The Greek composition follows the Semitic image by uniting the number and duration to create an adjective specifically designating this great age.
G1541.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 4:19, where Paul speaks of Abraham. It serves to emphasize the extraordinary age of the patriarch at the time when the promise of the birth of Isaac was to be fulfilled. This unique and precise usage shows that the author chose this specific term to insist on the apparent impossibility of the event: a one-hundred-year-old man cannot naturally father a child. This context of paradoxical faith — believing in the impossible — is the key to this remarkable usage.
G1541.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the power of faith in the face of the impossible. Abraham, at the age when all procreation becomes humanly inconceivable, believes in God's promise. For the Christian, this centenarian age becomes a symbol of those situations where reason and experience say "it's impossible," but faith asserts "God can." This passage teaches that true faith does not look at obstacles, but at the faithfulness and power of the One who promises.

sens: One hundred times more, one hundred times as much
Extraordinary multiplication of a quantity or a reward
Abundance surpassing all expectations
G1542.detail:
1. The word literally means "one hundred times": if you possess something and receive it a hundredfold, you receive one hundred times the initial amount. Jesus uses this word to describe the extraordinary fruit of the seed that falls on good soil (Luke 8:8): a single seed produces a hundred times its seed.
2. In Jesus' promises to the disciples, the hundredfold signifies an immense reward for the sacrifice made. Whoever has left everything to follow Jesus "will receive a hundredfold" (Matthew 19:29), meaning one hundred times more than what they have given up: brothers, sisters, a mother, children, lands.
3. This notion of a hundredfold emphasizes the unimaginable abundance of divine generosity. Mark adds an important nuance: this reward is received "presently in this age" (Mark 10:30), "with persecutions," and then "in the age to come, eternal life." The hundredfold is not a naive promise of material wealth, but the certainty that God gives back beyond all measure.
G1542.origine: The Greek word ἑκατονταπλασίων comes from two elements: ἑκατόν (hundred) and πλάσιον (times, multiplier). It is a compound that expresses the idea of multiplication or multiplicity. The Greek word here translates divine abundance in the Old Testament, often linked to the blessing and fertility promised by God to His people.
G1542.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, in contexts of promise and blessing. In Matthew 19:29, Jesus responds to Peter's question about what the disciples will receive in exchange for sacrificing everything: the hundredfold. In Mark 10:30, the same teaching is reiterated with more details about the blessings of the Christian community and the addition of persecutions. In Luke 8:8, it is the parable of the sower where the good soil produces fruit a hundredfold, illustrating the supernatural fertility of the Kingdom. The hundredfold symbolizes in all cases a blessing disproportionate to the initial investment.
G1542.portee: For the believer, the hundredfold is not a guarantee of material wealth, but an assurance that God does not leave any sacrifice unrewarded. Those who accept losses for the Kingdom receive an incomparable compensation, not only in this world (through the fellowship of the Church and spiritual blessings), but also in eternity. This word frees the disciple from economic fear and encourages radical trust in God.

sens: Roman military officer who commands one hundred soldiers
Man of rank intermediate between soldier and tribune
Military officer responsible for executing orders and maintaining guard
Man of power and authority in the Roman army
G1543.detail:
1. The centurion is a Roman military officer commanding a hundred soldiers — literally, his name comes from "cent" and means one who commands one hundred men. It is an intermediate rank: not a mere soldier, nor a supreme commander (the tribune), but a field officer with authority and responsibility.
2. In the Gospel, the centurion of Capernaum comes to plead with Jesus for his sick servant (Matthew 8:5), and shows remarkable faith by recognizing Jesus' authority. He is a man accustomed to giving orders and understanding authority: "I say to one, Go, and he goes" (Matthew 8:9).
3. At the crucifixion, the centurion guarding Jesus, seeing the earthquake and Jesus' death, confesses: "Truly, this man was the Son of God" (Matthew 27:54). Another centurion at the cross glorifies God (Luke 23:47).
4. In Acts, centurions mainly appear as executors of Roman orders: they escort prisoners, maintain order, enforce Roman law.
G1543.origine: The Greek word ἑκατόνταρχος (hekatontarchos) is composed of two roots: ἑκατόν (hekat-on, "hundred") and ἄρχω (arch-ō, "to command"). It literally designates one who commands one hundred men. In the Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, the Greek texts use this word to translate מֵאָה שַׂר (méah sar, literally "prince of the hundred" or "chief of the hundred"), which also referred to a military officer in the Jewish context. The word holds particular importance in the New Testament as an interface between the occupying Roman world and the occupied Jews.
G1543.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. In Matthew and Luke, the centurions encountered are notable individuals: the one who comes to Jesus for his servant (Matthew 8:5-13, Luke 7:2-10), those who guard Jesus at the cross (Matthew 27:54, Luke 23:47). In Acts, the word designates the officers who escort Paul as a prisoner — notably Julius, the centurion of the Augustan cohort (Acts 27:1) — or those who maintain order in Jerusalem (Acts 21:32). Centurions also appear as receptive to the Gospel: Cornelius the centurion of Caesarea (Acts 10:1-22) becomes one of the first non-Jewish converts.
G1543.portee: The centurion embodies a figure of unexpected conversion: despite his Roman uniform and military authority, he can recognize the power of God and the truth of Jesus. For the believer, these accounts show that no human position — not even military power and authority — excludes one from the grace of God. The centurion of Capernaum also illustrates how humility and faith often come from unexpected places.

sens: To expel someone or something from a place with authority or force
To command someone or something to leave, to go away
To reject, to push away, to refuse
To remove, to take out, to pull something from a place
G1544.detail:
1. To expel someone or something from a place with authority or force: it means to put outside, dismiss, banish. Jesus casts out the merchants from the temple (Mark 11:15); demons are cast out from the possessed (Mark 1:34); an unworthy servant is cast out from the master's presence (Matthew 25:30).

2. To command someone or something to leave, to go away, to give the order to withdraw: this is a milder sense than the first, meaning to direct, to send. Jesus sends His disciples on a mission (Luke 10:2, "Pray the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers").

3. To reject, to push away, to refuse: it means to dismiss, to disavow. A man born blind is cast out of the synagogue for defending Jesus (John 9:34).

4. To remove, to take out, to pull something from a place: to take a speck out of one's eye (Matthew 7:4), to pluck out the eye that causes offense (Mark 9:47), to take money from one's purse (Luke 10:35).
G1544.origine: The word comes from ἐκ ("out of") and βάλλω ("to throw, to cast"). The initial image is that of a force projecting something outward. In classical Greek, this compound verb already expresses the idea of expulsion and rejection. In the Greek version of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), it translates several Hebrew verbs: גָּרַשׁ ("to cast out"), שָׁלַךְ ("to throw"), יָצָא ("to go out"), all of which reinforce this notion of removal.
G1544.emploi: The verb is very frequent in the New Testament (76 occurrences). The Gospels make extensive use of it to describe the powerful action of Jesus: casting out demons (Matthew 7:22; Mark 1:34) is a central act of His ministry that manifests His victory over evil. It also applies to the expulsion from the temple (Matthew 21:12; Luke 19:45) and to fraternal correction (removing a speck from one's eye, Matthew 7:4-5). The verb also designates acts of human rejection: John 9:34 reports that the Pharisees cast out the healed blind man. The moral usage is present: to reject the name of the disciples (Luke 6:22), or to exclude someone from the assembly (3 John 10). The tone varies from direct command (Luke 10:2: sending out laborers) to violence or rejection.
G1544.portee: Understanding this word illuminates Jesus' power over the spirit world and His dominion over evil. The expulsion of demons shows that the Kingdom of God triumphs over evil: what enters into Jesus is not defiled, but what comes out can be (Matthew 15:17-18). The word also invites the believer to self-judgment: to remove the beam from one's own eye before correcting a brother. Finally, the rejection of the disciples by the world (Luke 6:22) places the disciple in communion with the fate of the Master.

sens: an opening or passage that allows one to escape a difficult situation
the outcome or final result of a situation
the resolution of a life or destiny
G1545.detail:
1. An exit is primarily a concrete way out, a path that allows one to escape or extricate oneself from difficulty. In 1 Corinthians 10:13, Paul assures that God always provides an "exit" alongside temptation: He never locks us in without giving us a way out, an escape route.
2. The word also designates the outcome or final result that a situation leads to. It is less about the action of exiting than the resolution itself, what results at the end.
3. In Hebrews 13:7, the "exit" of your leaders' lives means the end of their lives, their fulfilled destiny — how their story concluded and what legacy they left behind.
G1545.origine: The Greek word comes from the root "ek-" (to go out, outside) and "basis" (the action of walking, standing). It paints the image of an exit, a passage outward. The family of the word notably includes the verb "ekbaïnô" (to go out, to leave). This root always evokes the idea of a crossing, of overcoming an obstacle.
G1545.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two provided passages. In 1 Corinthians 10:13, Paul uses it to affirm that God never leaves the believer without resources in the face of temptation: He always prepares an "exit," a concrete means of not succumbing. In Hebrews 13:7, the word designates the "end" of the lives of those who taught you the Word — their death, but especially the way their lives concluded in faithfulness. In both cases, it is a comforting word: it speaks of an exit (in Paul) or a visible conclusion (in the author of Hebrews).
G1545.portee: This word encourages the tempted or tested believer: it reminds us that God never allows a trial without providing an exit, a way of salvation or faithfulness. It is also an invitation to observe how the believers before us completed their race — their lives as a testimony — to imitate their faith. The exit is never closed.

sens: the act of throwing (a cargo) into the sea
cargo thrown overboard
that which is thrown away, rejected
G1546.detail:
1. This is the Greek word that describes the act of throwing something overboard from a ship. The word comes from the verb "to throw out" and the prefix "out of." In Acts 27:18, during the terrible storm that shakes Paul's ship, the sailors throw the cargo into the sea to lighten the boat and keep it afloat — it is an act of desperation in the face of extreme danger.
2. The word can also refer to the cargo itself, the totality of goods that are thrown into the sea. This meaning applies in the shipwreck narrative: it speaks of "the cargo" that is abandoned to save the ship and the lives on board.
3. In a broader sense, it simply refers to what is rejected, what is thrown out: the action and its result are designated by the same Greek word.
G1546.origine: The word comes from the verb "ekballô" (to throw out, to expel): "ek" means "out of" and "ballô" means "to throw." The Greek word literally describes the act of projecting something outside, particularly out of a boat. It is a concrete term that paints the image of a quick and necessary action in the face of maritime panic.
G1546.emploi: The word "ekbolê" appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 27:18, at the heart of the dramatic account of Paul's shipwreck on his way to Rome. Luke reports how, after two days of violent storm, the crew begins to throw overboard everything that can be to save the ship. The context shows urgency and distress: this is not an ordinary unloading, but a massive abandonment of precious cargo for survival. The Greek word thus emphasizes the desperate action of the sailors in the face of a situation that escapes all human control.
G1546.portee: This passage reminds the believer that, in the storms of life, sometimes we must accept losing what seems precious to save what is essential. Paul, in the midst of chaos, remains firm in his faith: God assured him that everyone would reach safety. For us today, this scene invites the early readers to see that even in shipwreck, God preserves His people, for it is His promise that matters, not our possessions or material securities.

sens: a child born of a child
descendant of a younger generation
heir of the family
G1549.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a child born of a previous generation — literally one who is "born of" (ἐκ-) someone. It is a grandchild, the son or daughter of a son or daughter (1 Timothy 5:4).
2. In a broader sense, it can refer to any descendant, meaning the children of our children or even the following generations that perpetuate the family line.
3. In biblical usage, the word is also used to designate one who inherits the name and responsibilities of their family — one who continues what their ancestors began.
G1549.origine: The word comes from the prefix ἐκ (ek, "out of, from") and the verb γίγνομαι (gignomai, "to be born"). Literally: "born of." This same root is found in other Greek words of the New Testament that express birth or origin. The Hebrew word פְּרִי (peri, "fruit") sometimes expresses this as well, as descent is seen as the "fruit" of the previous generation.
G1549.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Timothy 5:4. Paul addresses young widows and their responsibilities toward their family: if a widow has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to honor their own and repay their parents for what they have received. It is a context of family ethics and recognition of each person's duty to those who have gone before. The contrast "children or grandchildren" shows that the word designates a later generation, more distant.
G1549.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith does not stop at a single generation: everyone is called to pass on what they have received to their descendants. The mention of grandchildren invites the believer to think far ahead, to see their family responsibility as a legacy that extends over several generations. It is a call to cultivate piety in families, not for oneself alone, but for those who will come after.

sens: To spend without reserve, to dedicate all one's resources or energy to someone or something
To give of oneself without counting the cost, to personally sacrifice
To exhaust one's resources in service to others
G1550.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of spending, consuming one's resources: money, possessions, strength. The prefix intensifies the idea — it is a total expenditure, without restraint. Paul speaks of expending himself very willingly for the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 12:15), showing his readiness to give materially.
2. In its reflexive sense (when the verb turns back on the subject), the word means to give oneself, to put one's own person at the service of others. Paul adds: "and I will expend myself" — not only his possessions, but himself, his energy, his time, his heart for the spiritual well-being of these Christians.
3. The image that emerges is one of love that keeps nothing for itself, that goes to the point of exhaustion. The context shows that Paul even accepts that this generous love may cost him the affection of the Corinthians, if necessary.
G1550.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐκ (ek: out of, outside) and the verb δαπανάω (dapanaō: to spend, to consume). This composition reinforces the simple idea of expenditure into a complete, exhaustive spending. The root evokes the action of drawing or consuming, as one consumes a resource until it is exhausted.
G1550.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:15. Paul uses it to describe his pastoral commitment to the Corinthians in a context of defending his apostleship. He asserts that he will even spend his own life for them, and this without regret, even if his love is not reciprocated. The word captures the selflessness and totality of the apostle's sacrifice: it is not a limited gift, it is an offering of oneself.
G1550.portee: This word from Paul invites the believer to reflect on the true nature of love: to love is not to calculate, to hold back, or to expect something in return. It is to give without limit, putting one's own existence at the service of others. For a spiritual leader or a disciple of Christ, this text reminds us that following Jesus may require total self-expenditure, just as Jesus himself expended himself on the cross for us.

sens: to receive or welcome someone or something that is coming
to remain in expectation, in waiting
to watch for the arrival of someone
G1551.detail:
1. In its primary sense, the word denotes the act of receiving something or someone that is arriving: it is an active waiting, directed towards the one who is coming. When Paul was waiting for Timothy in Corinth (1 Corinthians 16:11), he was watching for him to welcome him.
2. By extension, it means to remain in an attitude of waiting, suspended on what is to happen. The sick by the pool of Bethesda were waiting for the movement of the water that would heal them (John 5:3), motionless and vigilant. Abraham was waiting for the heavenly city (Hebrews 11:10), keeping his heart turned towards God's promise.
3. The word can also mean to wait for someone or something with impatience, somewhat like spying. In church meetings, the Corinthians were to wait for one another (1 Corinthians 11:33): to mutually respect each other while waiting for everyone to be present before eating.
G1551.origine: The word comes from the prefix "ek" (out of, outside) added to "dechomai" (to receive, to welcome). This composition creates the image of "receiving from outside" or "going to meet what is coming." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it sometimes translates words meaning "to wait" (like erèv, to wait for evening, or qabats, to gather). It is a waiting that is not passive: it implies a certain tension, a vigilance directed towards what is coming.
G1551.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles (Acts, 1 Corinthians, Hebrews, James). It carries three nuances depending on the context: first, a concrete and immediate waiting (Paul waiting for Timothy, the sick waiting for the healing water), then a deeper and more patient spiritual waiting (Abraham waiting for the heavenly city, Christ waiting for his enemies to bow), and finally, a waiting related to courtesy and mutual respect (the Corinthians waiting for one another at the table). The word always emphasizes vigilance: the one who waits is never indifferent.
G1551.portee: This word invites the believer to understand that biblical waiting is not passivity, but an active and vigilant posture. To wait on God or His promises is to keep the mind turned towards Him, the heart open and ready. It is also a call to mutual respect in church life: to wait for others is to honor them.

sens: Which is clear, obvious, visible to all
Which cannot be hidden or contested
G1552.detail:
1. Manifest means "obvious, clear, easily seen." It is something that stands out. In 2 Timothy 3:9, Paul asserts that the folly of the adversaries of the Gospel will be "manifest to all": everyone will see and recognize their error, just as one sees the light of day.
2. Manifest also means "impossible to deny or hide." It is a character that imposes itself, which cannot be contested. The folly that Paul speaks of cannot remain secret or doubtful: it becomes visible and undeniable to everyone.
G1552.origine: The Greek word ἔκδηλος (ekdēlos) is formed from ἔκ (ek, "out of, from") and δῆλος (dēlos, "clear, visible"). The prefix ἔκ reinforces the meaning: it is "very clear," "clearly visible." It is an intensified form of the word δῆλος, from which the French word "didactic" also derives in a distant genealogy. Biblical Greek borrows here from a simple image: what is outside (ἔκ), what comes out of the shadow, is visible to all.
G1552.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:9. Paul uses it to describe how the falsehood of the adversaries will ultimately be publicly exposed. It is a strong word, emphasizing that the evidence of truth or error imposes itself on everyone, without exception. It is an intensified form of the word "clear," which highlights the irresistible and universal nature of revelation.
G1552.portee: This word reminds us that the truth cannot remain hidden indefinitely: it comes to light. For the believer, it is an assurance: the lies of false teachers will one day be visible to all. It also calls for vigilance: if a doctrine is truly contrary to the Gospel, time and facts will reveal it.

sens: to be absent from one's home, from one's usual place
to be separated from someone or something
to go away, to leave from
G1553.detail:
1. The word means literally to be far from one's dwelling: the idea of departure and absence. In 2 Corinthians 5:6, Paul says that as long as we remain in this body, we are "far from the Lord" — it should be understood as: we are absent from His presence, we are separated from Him by the death that awaits us.
2. More broadly, it describes the state of separation: one leaves a place, one distances oneself from it. This meaning appears in 2 Corinthians 5:8, where Paul would prefer to "leave this body" to be with the Lord — it refers to death, the definitive departure from this life.
3. The verb can also simply mean to leave, to go away from a place. In 2 Corinthians 5:9, Paul speaks of striving to please the Lord "whether we remain or whether we leave" — that is, whether we stay in this body or depart from it.
G1553.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἔκδημος (ekdèmos), formed from ἐκ (ek, "out of") and δῆμος (dèmos, "the house, the country"). The image is that of going out of one's home, distancing oneself from one's dwelling. Its opposite is ἐνδημέω (endèmeô), "to be at home, to reside." It is a common Greek vocabulary word used to speak of absence and separation.
G1553.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the passage of 2 Corinthians 5:6-9 where Paul reflects on the condition of the Christian living in the body. He plays on the contrast: as long as we live on earth in this body, we are "far from the Lord" (absent from Him), but if we leave (through death), we will be with Him. The word thus applies to spiritual separation from God and the perspective of death as a passage into His presence. Paul uses this vocabulary to urge believers to live in view of the Lord in anticipation of this meeting.
G1553.portee: This word invites the Christian to become aware of their current condition: although saved in Christ, we still live far from the visible presence of the Lord. This gives meaning to our faith and current perseverance — we long to meet Him face to face. The word also reminds us that death is not an end for the believer, but a "departure" from this body to finally enter the presence of the Lord.

sens: To hand something over to someone for them to exploit for a rent or fee
To entrust a property, an asset to a third party who profits from it
To rely on someone else for the management of an asset
G1554.detail:
1. To lease means to rent out a property (a vineyard, land) to someone else who exploits it and profits from it, in exchange for a rent or a share of the harvest. It is a contract of exploitation: the owner temporarily cedes the use to a farmer, who must pay what is agreed. In Jesus' parable, the master of the house "leases" his vineyard to tenants (Matthew 21:33), who cultivate the vineyard and must give him "the produce at harvest time" (Luke 20:9).

2. More broadly, it means to abandon, entrust, hand something over to someone else — the word can also mean "to yield" or "to deliver." In the parable, when the owner "leases" the vineyard, he transfers the daily management to the tenants.
G1554.origine: The word is composed of ἐκ ("out of," "outside") and δίδωμι ("to give"). The image is that of giving something to someone else, with the notion of handing over, of transmission. In biblical Hebrew, similar words like נָתַן (natan, "to give") express this idea of handing over an asset.
G1554.emploi: This verb appears only 4 times in the New Testament, solely in the parable of the vineyard among the three evangelists (Matthew 21:33 and 41; Mark 12:1; Luke 20:9). Jesus uses it to tell the story of an owner who plants a beautiful vineyard, surrounds it with a hedge, adds a winepress and a tower, and then entrusts it to tenants. The meaning is very concrete: it refers to a real agricultural and commercial practice in Jesus' time. But Jesus uses this image to speak of God's relationship with Israel — the vineyard represents the people, and the tenants are the religious leaders supposed to take care of it.
G1554.portee: This parable teaches that God entrusts His gifts to those He chooses, and that He expects an account. Leasing a vineyard means receiving a responsibility: the tenants are not owners; they are managers. For the reader, the word invites reflection on how we manage what God entrusts to us — our talents, our possessions, our responsibilities. We are like farmers of the Kingdom: our hands hold only temporarily what belongs to God.

sens: To report, to expose by narrative what one has seen or knows
To make known publicly, to announce
To narrate a series of facts or events in a developed manner
G1555.detail:
1. The verb means to recount, to report, to make known by presenting the facts in a complete and detailed manner. It is to put into words what one has seen, heard, or experienced. In Acts 15:3, the apostles "recounted" the conversion of the Gentiles at each stage of their journey, providing the details of this wonder.

2. It also means to announce publicly, to widely make known. The purpose is not to report confidentially, but to declare to all. In Acts 13:41, the prophet Habakkuk "recounted" what God was going to accomplish, not as a simple narrative, but as a word from God addressed to the crowd.

3. More broadly, it is to unfold a narrative over time and in its details: to enumerate the facts, the episodes, the stages of a story. The verb emphasizes less the act of speaking than the completeness and order of the narrative.
G1555.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: *ek* ("out of, completely"), *dia* ("through"), and *hēgeomai* ("to lead, guide, recount"). This construction emphasizes the idea of fully unfolding, leading through, bringing to light. The simple verb *hēgeomai* already means "to recount"; the prefix *ekdia* intensifies it. In Acts, this term makes visible the public transmission of the Good News.
G1555.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Acts of the Apostles. In Acts 13:41, it appears in a quotation from the Old Testament (Habakkuk 1:5 according to the Greek translation) where God announces His work to the unbelievers. In Acts 15:3, Paul's companions and Barnabas "recount" to the church the conversion of the Gentiles during their journey. In both cases, the verb denotes the public announcement and detailed exposition of an important event. The context emphasizes that this is not a rumor, but a word intended to be widely shared and heard.
G1555.portee: This word shows how faith is transmitted: not through short formulas, but through the living and detailed recounting of what God has done. To recount in detail what God accomplishes is to allow others to fully understand His intervention and to be transformed by it. The Christian is thus invited to share their testimony not superficially, but by bringing to light the different stages and depth of it.

sens: To administer justice on behalf of someone who has been wronged or treated unjustly
To punish someone for a transgression or disobedience
To retaliate against an affront by seeking restitution
To claim one's rights, to obtain satisfaction before a judge
G1556.detail:
1. To administer justice on behalf of someone who has been victimized: this involves intervening to defend someone who has suffered harm or aggression. The widow in Luke 18:3 and 5 asks the judge to "avenge" her against her adversary — she demands that the wrong done to her be rectified.
2. To punish a transgression or disobedience: the term then refers to the sanction that follows a wrongful act. In 2 Corinthians 10:6, Paul speaks of "punishing every disobedience."
3. To retaliate against an outrage or injustice: this involves seeking vengeance, demanding that the aggressor pay for their act. Revelation 6:10 shows the martyrs crying out, "How long… will you refrain from avenging our blood?"
4. To claim one's rights through a just intervention: the verb combines the idea of defending the victim and punishing the guilty party. In Revelation 19:2, God "has avenged the blood of His servants" by demanding it from the guilty — He has restored justice.
G1556.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἔκδικος (an "advocate" or one who defends the right), itself composed of ἐκ ("out of, entirely") and δίκη ("justice, right"). The basic image is that of "bringing the right out into the open," meaning to assert it, to claim it openly. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate the Hebrew פָּקַד (to visit, to punish), נָקַם (to take vengeance), and שָׁפַט (to judge, to render justice).
G1556.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament. It has two main nuances: on one hand, the request for civil justice (Luke 18:3, 5: a widow imploring a judge), on the other hand, the judicial action of God or His representatives in the face of guilt (Romans 12:19: prohibition against taking vengeance oneself; 2 Corinthians 10:6: punishing disobedience; Revelation 6:10 and 19:2: God avenging against enemies). The Pauline context emphasizes that only the authority (magistrate or God) has the right to avenge; the Segond translates it sometimes as "avenge," sometimes as "administer justice" or "punish" depending on the nuance intended.
G1556.portee: This word reminds Christians that they should not take it upon themselves to punish or seek vengeance: only the established authority (magistrate) or God Himself has the power and right to do so. It also comforts the oppressed by showing them that God is a judge and does not leave unpunished the evil done against His children — not out of sadism, but to restore justice and the honor of His creation.

sens: The act of punishing someone who has done wrong, to administer justice to someone who has been wronged
The act of divine retribution, God's anger that punishes sin
The defense of the rights of someone suffering injustice
G1557.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the act of punishing someone who has committed a wrongful act, restoring order after an offense. It conveys the idea of making the guilty party pay for their act. In Acts 7:24, Moses "avenges" the one who is mistreated by striking the Egyptian who wrongs him.
2. In the Bible, vengeance is often presented as the work of God Himself, who punishes sin with justice. In Romans 12:19, Paul reminds that "vengeance" belongs to the Lord alone, and not to men. It is God who recompenses, who responds to evil with punishment.
3. The word can also express the idea of justice rendered to those who suffer. In Luke 18:7-8, Jesus speaks of the "justice" that God will grant to His elect who cry out to Him: it involves defending their rights, protecting them against injustice. In Luke 21:22, the "days of vengeance" are the times when God executes His judgments.
G1557.origine: The word comes from the root "ek" ("out of, from") and "diké" ("justice, judgment"). The basic idea is: to bring justice out, to manifest justice in action. The corresponding Hebrew word used in the Greek Old Testament is "naqam" (נָקָם), which means "to avenge, to punish." The family of the Greek word includes "ekdikéo" ("to avenge"), of which "ekdikèsis" is the noun form.
G1557.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. It is used in three main contexts: first to describe God's action in judging and punishing evil (Luke 21:22; Romans 12:19; 2 Thessalonians 1:8; Hebrews 10:30); secondly, to evoke the justice that God renders to those who suffer injustice and cry out to Him (Luke 18:7-8); finally, to speak of the judicial punishment that public authority inflicts (1 Peter 2:14; Acts 7:24). The word thus oscillates between the idea of punishing the guilty and that of protecting the victim: God "avenges" both by punishing evil and restoring rights.
G1557.portee: This word reminds Christians that justice belongs to God alone, and that we should not take it upon ourselves through personal vengeance. It also assures those who suffer injustice that God hears them and will intervene to defend them. Finally, it proclaims that God does not ignore sin and will judge with justice, which should lead us to repentance.

sens: Punishment inflicted to rectify a wrong or to punish a crime
The act of avenging an offense or injustice
The role of one who exercises the right to punish
G1558.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the punishment inflicted on someone to rectify a wrong or to punish a wrongful act — the idea of retribution, of deserved penalty. In Romans 13:4, the magistrate bears the sword "to execute vengeance" against the one who does evil: this is his official function to punish crimes.
2. By extension, it is the act of administering justice in response to an offense, to render to someone according to their deeds. In 1 Thessalonians 4:6, the Lord "avenges" fraud and greed: God Himself takes charge of punishing those who do wrong to their brothers.
3. The word can also refer to the person or authority that exercises this punitive judgment — the one who avenges, who rectifies wrongs. But in the two Pauline usages, it is primarily the act of punishment that is in view.
G1558.origine: The Greek word comes from the root δίκη (dike, justice, right). The prefix ἐκ- (ek-, out of, outside) reinforces the idea: vengeance is justice that comes out into the open, that manifests and strikes. In Greek, the word evokes less personal anger than the exercise of the right to punish — justice being enacted.
G1558.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul. In Romans 13:4, it qualifies the role of the civil magistrate: he is a servant of God who executes vengeance against the wrongdoer — a legitimate and necessary function. In 1 Thessalonians 4:6, Paul reminds believers that the Lord Himself avenges fraud and greed among brothers — God does not leave evil unpunished. In both cases, vengeance is not a private act of anger, but an official justice: that of the state or that of God.
G1558.portee: This word teaches Christians that the punishment of evil is not a personal vengeance or hatred, but a legitimate act of justice reserved for authority — civil or divine. The believer should not take vengeance themselves, as it is the matter of God and those He has established to maintain order. Vengeance, understood as just retribution, is an act of justice that God Himself exercises with certainty.

sens: Chase or expel someone with violence
Pursue someone to harm them or prevent them from acting
Harass or torment someone because of their faith or convictions
G1559.detail:
1. The literal meaning of the word is "to chase," "to expel": it is the action of forcing someone to leave a place or to flee from a threat.
2. The word is used to denote the act of actively pursuing someone to harm them: they are tracked, tormented, sought to be eliminated or arrested.
3. In the biblical context, especially for the disciples of Jesus, to persecute means to attack someone because they believe in Christ or follow His message: it is hostility motivated by faith. This is how Paul describes in 1 Thessalonians 2:15 how the unbelieving Jews "persecuted us" — they actively tormented the early Christians to make them cease.
G1559.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "ek" ("out of," "outside") and the verb "diōkō" ("to chase," "to pursue"). This composition emphasizes intensity: it is not just to pursue, but to pursue to drive out, to expel. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates Hebrew verbs that express forced flight or violent expulsion.
G1559.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:15. Paul uses it to remind the Thessalonians how the unbelieving Jews persecuted the early Church — not just with words, but through sustained and hostile action. The context shows that this persecution is part of a broader opposition: these same Jews killed Jesus and the prophets, and now they oppose the Christians. The word thus denotes active, organized, and repeated hostility.
G1559.portee: This word reminds Christians that faith in Jesus can provoke active opposition, even from those who claim religious tradition. It also encourages recognition that suffering for Christ is a reality attested from the origins of the Church, and not an anomaly. This helps the believer understand that persecution is a test of the sincerity of faith.

sens: Handed over to someone
Abandoned to a fate
Destined to undergo
G1560.detail:
1. The word describes the action of handing someone or something over to a person or authority. It is to be "delivered" into the power of someone else. In Acts 2:23, Jesus is described as delivered: handed over to those who crucified Him.
2. The word can also express the idea of being abandoned to a fate, ceded defenseless. It is a form of renunciation where one has no control or no longer has control.
3. Figuratively, the word expresses a destiny: to be delivered to something means to be exposed to it or to be doomed to it. One undergoes what one has been delivered to.
G1560.origine: The word comes from two parts: "ék" ("out of," "from") and "dotos" ("given"). It thus designates what is given or handed over from a starting point. It is an adjective formed from the verb "ekdídômi" (to hand over, to deliver). The word expresses an active cession: someone delivers something or someone else to a destination or to a person.
G1560.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 2:23. Peter uses it to describe Jesus as having been "delivered" by a predetermined plan and foreknowledge of God, then crucified by wicked hands. It is a judicial and political term: it designates the handing over of a prisoner or a condemned person. In this context, it emphasizes both historical responsibility and divine purpose in the Passion.
G1560.portee: This word reveals a profound tension at the heart of the Gospel: Jesus was delivered according to God's purpose, and yet men bear the responsibility for it. For the believer, this reality teaches that the cross is not an accident, but an act of God accomplished in human history. It invites reflection on divine sovereignty and human responsibility in the mystery of salvation.

sens: State of mind of someone who is waiting for something, who anticipates an event
Feeling of anxiety or fear in the face of a dreaded event
G1561.detail:
1. The word designates the state of someone who is waiting, looking towards the future while anticipating an event. It is the attitude of someone who is reaching for something that is to come. In Hebrews 10:27, Paul speaks of an "expectation": that of the rebels who await God's judgment, knowing that something is inevitably coming.

2. In this context, the "expectation" takes on a dramatic hue — it is anxiety, fearful dread before what is to come. The rebels who have rejected the Son of God no longer await a blessing: they await condemnation, "the fury of a fire that will consume." The expectation then becomes synonymous with terror.
G1561.origine: The word comes from the verb "ekdechomai" (to welcome, receive, wait) formed from "ek" (from, out of) and "dechomai" (to receive). The primary idea is that of "receiving from" or "succeeding to," but it has developed to mean "to wait" — to wait is in a sense to "mentally receive" the event that is coming. In classical Greek, the word could also designate an interpretation or a succession, but the New Testament uses it solely in the sense of "expectation" or "anticipation."
G1561.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 10:27. Paul uses it to paint the psychological state of the rebels who have despised the sacrifice of the Son of God. The "expectation" he describes is not a peaceful or joyful waiting, but a waiting filled with dread — they know that a terrible judgment awaits them. This context shows that the word here carries the idea of an anxious, almost oppressive anticipation of punishment.
G1561.portee: This word reminds us of a fundamental biblical truth: God's judgment is real and inevitable for those who reject Christ. There is no possible escape. For the believer, this truth invites recognition of the grace received in Jesus; for the one who refuses, it underscores the gravity of their choice: they can only dread what is to come.

sens: Take off a garment from someone, undress them
Strip someone of their possessions, steal or rob them
Figuratively, to strip oneself of something, to part with or abandon it
G1562.detail:
1. To remove a garment from someone means to undress or disrobe them: it is the action of taking away the clothes that a person is wearing. The soldiers who crucify Jesus take off His clothes to cover Him with a purple robe in mockery (Matthew 27:28), then they take off this robe and return His clothes to Him (Matthew 27:31).
2. To strip means to take away everything someone possesses: to steal or seize their belongings. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the traveler "fell among thieves, who stripped him, and wounded him" (Luke 10:30): it is the same word that describes both the theft of his possessions and the assault.
3. Figuratively, to strip or to undress can express the idea of abandoning something essential: Paul speaks of "stripping off" the mortal body, that is, leaving it at death to "be clothed" with the resurrected body (2 Corinthians 5:4).
G1562.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: ἐκ ("out of") and δύω ("to enter, to put on"), literally meaning "to make come out of." In Hebrew, it corresponds mainly to פָּשַׁט ("to remove, to take off, to strip"). This image of a garment being removed or of a possession being seized is very concrete in the everyday language of the Mediterranean peoples.
G1562.emploi: The verb appears six times in the New Testament. Four occurrences describe the physical action of removing Jesus' clothes before the crucifixion (Matthew 27:28, 27:31, Mark 15:20) or of travelers by robbers (Luke 10:30). Once, the word is used in the passive form to say "to be clothed" (2 Corinthians 5:3, reverse sense: "found clothed"). Finally, in the middle (reflexive) form, it designates the action of stripping oneself, in the figurative sense of the body (2 Corinthians 5:4). The context of the Passion dominates the usage, but Paul applies it to the condition of the soul after death.
G1562.portee: This word helps us meditate on the humiliation of Jesus: to remove His clothes is to strip Him of His human dignity, an act of mockery and cruelty. When we read "they took off His clothes," we see the abasement of the Son of God. For the believer, the image of stripping also speaks of renunciation: leaving the temporal to put on the eternal, what Paul calls the passage from death to resurrection.

sens: at that place, in that location
toward that place, to go there
in this context or situation
G1563.detail:
1. The primary and most common meaning is spatial and concrete: "there" designates a specific place, a location where one is or where something is happening. It simply indicates a location in space. For example, in Matthew 24:51, Jesus speaks of the unfaithful servant: "there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth" — the word "there" refers to the place of punishment he has just mentioned. Similarly, in John 19:42, "It was there that they laid Jesus" — it is the nearby tomb that has just been discussed.
2. With movement verbs (to go, to come, to head), "there" indicates direction, the point toward which one is heading, as a synonym for "to go there." In Matthew 2:22, it is said that Joseph "withdrew to the districts of Galilee" (and went there) — it is no longer just a location, but an action of going toward that location. In John 4:40, the Samaritans ask Jesus to "stay with them" and "he stayed there two days."
3. The word can also mark a position in a context or situation: "at this point in the narrative" or "in these circumstances." In Mark 11:5, "some of those who were there" — that is, present at that moment, in that scene — intervene in the drama.
G1563.origine: The Greek word ἐκεῖ (ekei) is an adverb of place formed from the root ἐκ ("from, out of"). Its basic image is that of a direction or point in space: "from there" becoming simply "there." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it primarily translates שָׁם (shàm), which has exactly the same meaning — a simple adverb of location. It is a fundamental and ancient word for speaking about space in both Greek and Hebrew.
G1563.emploi: The word ekei appears 98 times in the New Testament, mostly in the four gospels and with remarkable frequency in Matthew. It is a very ordinary adverb, without particular theological nuance: its role is purely to situate the action or state in space. In Matthew 2:13, the angel tells Joseph to flee to Egypt and stay there; in Matthew 8:12 and parallels, "there" designates the place of judgment, the outer darkness. In John 11:31, "there" indicates where the disciples think Jesus has gone. The word is sometimes redundant ("where... there"), notably in Revelation 12:6, 14, recalling the Hebrew construction שָׁם אֲשֶׁר. Its use is consistent across all contexts: narratives of movement, descriptions of places, locations of events.
G1563.portee: This humble and everyday word reminds us that the Gospel unfolds in the concrete: Jesus is not an abstract idea, but a person who moves from place to place, who stands somewhere, who acts in specific locations (at the well of Samaria, by the tomb of Lazarus, by the sea). This incarnation of salvation in space and time affirms that God touches the tangible reality where we live.

sens: from a given place, from that specific location
after that, then, subsequently
G1564.detail:
1. The word designates the spatial starting point: one leaves a place to go elsewhere. Jesus "departed from there" after teaching his disciples (Matthew 11:1), or "having gone a little farther" from a location (Mark 1:19). It conveys the idea of detaching from a known location to head toward another.

2. The word can also mark a succession in time: what comes after an event or action. Moreover, it means "subsequently" or "then" — a natural continuation of the narrative.
G1564.origine: The word is composed of "ek" ("out of") and "kei" ("there"), literally meaning "from this place." It is an adverb of place that expresses the source or starting point of an action. In Hebrew and Aramaic, שׁם (shàm, "there") is often found, which the Greek translation of the Old Testament renders appropriately with this word. The adverb "kei" is linked to a root indicating a fixed position.
G1564.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the New Testament, mostly in the gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and in Acts. It structures the narrative of the movements of Jesus and his apostles: Jesus "departed from there" to withdraw after learning of John the Baptist's death (Matthew 14:13), or to teach in another region (Mark 7:24). In Acts, it marks the stages of Paul's missionary journey. In Revelation 22:2, it situates the tree of life in the heavenly city. It is more an adverb of movement and itinerary than of time, even if it can suggest a succession.
G1564.portee: This word invites us to see how the Gospel spreads through movement: Jesus does not remain fixed, he moves, and "from there" he goes elsewhere to bring his message. For the reader, this reminds us that the Christian life is not static, but a journey following Christ. The expression also emphasizes that each event of the Good News is situated in a concrete place and moment: God acts in history, not in abstraction.

sens: What is distant in space or time, compared to what is close
Used to refer to a person or thing that has already been mentioned
Used emphatically to insist on someone or something
Marking an era, a period: that time
Used to refer to a person named or unnamed, often with a nuance of distance or detachment
Used adjectively with a noun determined by the article
G1565.detail:
1. This pronoun marks a distance or separation: it designates something that is far from the speaker or listener, unlike "this" which is close. "In those days John the Baptist appeared" (Matthew 3:1) — that time is far from us, it is a bygone era that is reported from afar.
2. It serves to refer back to a person or thing already mentioned to return to it: the reader has already heard it named, and it is designated again. It is a means of continuing the narrative while keeping its subject in mind.
3. Sometimes "this" is used forcefully to emphasize someone or something, to draw attention to it: it is a way of insisting, saying "that one precisely."
4. In front of a time indication (day, hour, year), "this" becomes "that time" or "that day": "the master will come on that day when he does not expect it" (Matthew 24:50).
5. It can refer to a person without naming them directly, either respectfully (when speaking of Christ) or with a certain distance or disdain. The absence of the name creates this effect.
6. As an adjective, it attaches to a noun and the preceding article to qualify it: "that city" (Luke 9:5), "that year" (John 18:13).
G1565.origine: This Greek pronoun comes from a root meaning "over there" (related to ἐκεῖ, "there"). Its starting image is that of distance, of "over there" opposed to "here." In classical Greek, it regularly contrasts with οὗτος ("this," "this one"), which marks proximity. In the Old Testament translated into Greek, it generally renders the Hebrew הוּא ("he," "that") and its variants, which function similarly to refer back to what has just been named or to mark distance.
G1565.emploi: This pronoun appears 247 times in the New Testament, particularly in Matthew and John. It is used mainly in three ways: first, it refers back to the subject of a sentence or an entire passage to keep it alive ("I know and am convinced in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself, and that a thing is unclean only for the one who thinks it unclean" in Romans 14:14); secondly, it designates a distant or future time, often the messianic era ("In those days John the Baptist appeared," Matthew 3:1, or "On that day," Matthew 7:22, speaking of Judgment); finally, it can mark a certain emotional or respectful distance regarding the person designated. Its meaning varies little: it is always the same grammatical work of reference and marking of distance.
G1565.portee: This pronoun teaches a discreet lesson: what is far from us — the past, the future, what does not belong to us — deserves to be designated with this mark of distance. When Scripture says "that day" in speaking of Judgment, it reminds us that it is a distinct event, which comes from God and not from us. This word also helps us read: every time it refers back to a character or action, it forces us to stay attentive to the thread of the narrative.

sens: At that place, in that location (idea of direction or location)
Towards that place, in that direction (movement)
In that country, that region (broader geographical sense)
G1566.detail:
1. The word designates a specific place, often referenced in the preceding context. In Acts 22:5, Paul speaks of the brothers "who were there" in Damascus: it is a defined location, where he was going to arrest them.
2. It can also express movement towards that place. The context of Acts 21:3 shows the ship heading "there," that is, to the port mentioned just before.
3. Sometimes the word broadens the perspective to an entire region, a country towards which one is going or where one is located, as in Paul's journey.
G1566.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that adds the suffix -σε (direction) to a word designating a place. It is a very common adverb of location, constructed to show both the place and the movement towards that place. In Greek, this suffix often indicates direction or destination.
G1566.emploi: The word appears twice in Acts. In Acts 21:3, it indicates a point of destination on Paul's journey. In Acts 22:5, used in a particular way, it qualifies "those who were there" — the believers in Damascus whom Paul was pursuing. It is a simple adverb, without major nuance from one use to another: it always anchors the action or presence in a specific place in the narrative.
G1566.portee: This small word reminds us that the events of the New Testament have concrete locations, real cities where people live. For the Christian reader, it is a call to see the reality of the apostolic testimony: Paul is truly going to Damascus, really pursuing believers who truly existed in that place. Faith is rooted in history.

sens: To seek someone or something with intention and effort
To actively search, rummage, examine in detail
To demand an account, require explanations or retribution
To solicit, desire to obtain something
G1567.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to seek someone or something: it is a directed search, aiming for a specific goal. In Acts 15:17, it is about seeking the Lord, searching for Him as one seeks someone they wish to find.

2. More concretely, to seek can mean to rummage, examine, scrutinize in depth to find what one is looking for. In 1 Peter 1:10, the prophets "searched and inquired" to understand the coming of Christ, examining the mystery of salvation from all angles.

3. In Luke 11:50-51, the word means to demand an account, to require retribution or vengeance: the blood of the prophets "will be required" of this generation, meaning that God will demand an account for it, He will claim retribution.

4. The word can also express a strong desire to obtain something. In Hebrews 12:17, Esau "sought" the blessing with tears, he insisted on obtaining it through his weeping.
G1567.origine: The word comes from ἐκ ("out of, outside") and ζητέω ("to seek, to try to find"). This composition gives the idea of a search that goes out from oneself, an active and sustained quest. In Hebrew, the word primarily renders דָּרַשׁ (darash), which means to inquire, seek, demand; this verb evokes a true effort to search and find. The family of the word also includes derivatives expressing intellectual search or questioning.
G1567.emploi: The word appears mainly in Paul and in the epistles. In Acts 15:17 and Romans 3:11, it describes humanity's search for God: God desires that people seek Him, but Romans 3:11 notes that no one truly seeks Him. In Hebrews 11:6, seeking God is linked to faith and the belief that He exists and rewards. In Luke 11:50-51, the word shifts from the sense of seeking to the sense of demanding retribution, vengeance: the murders of the prophets will be accounted for to this generation. In 1 Peter 1:10, the prophets sought to understand the revelations they transmitted. The word thus carries the idea of a directed quest, sometimes towards a person (God), sometimes towards understanding, sometimes towards retribution.
G1567.portee: Seeking God is not a passive or occasional act: it is an active, sustained endeavor that requires effort and commitment. The Bible calls believers to seek the Lord with all their heart (Acts 15:17, Hebrews 11:6). But it also reveals that the human heart, without God's grace, does not seek Him naturally (Romans 3:11): thus, seeking God is a sign of the faith that the Holy Spirit produces in us.

sens: To experience sudden and intense fear
To be astonished, surprised by something extraordinary
To be terrified, paralyzed by fear
G1568.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to experience a sudden fear that seizes the whole being: it is a vivid and immediate fear that stops us in our tracks. When the resurrected Jesus appears to the women at the tomb, they "were astonished" (Mark 16:5), so filled with terror and mixed astonishment by the event.
2. The word also expresses surprise mixed with fear: this double reaction that takes hold of us when we see something unexpected and troubling. After the transfiguration, "the crowd saw Jesus, and they were amazed" (Mark 9:15) — a mix of astonishment and disturbance.
3. In the passion, Jesus "began to be greatly distressed and troubled" (Mark 14:33): here the word describes a deep anguish, a terror that invades the soul in the face of what is to come.
G1568.origine: The word comes from the prefix "ek" (to go out, outside) and the root "thamb-" which evokes fear, astonishment: literally "to be thrown out of oneself by fear." It is a verb that expresses the idea of being shaken, internally disturbed. The root "thamb-" appears in classical Greek with the meaning of being stunned or shaken.
G1568.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Gospel of Mark, always to describe reactions to superhuman or extraordinary events. In Mark 9:15, it is the crowd's surprise at Jesus returning from the transfiguration. In Mark 14:33, Jesus Himself feels this fear in Gethsemane, facing the suffering that awaits Him. In Mark 16:5-6, the women at the tomb are seized with fear before the angel, then the angel reassures them: "Do not be afraid." Mark loves this verb to show how divine events shake humans.
G1568.portee: This word reminds us that encountering the divine is first about being seized, shaken, destabilized — even in the good news. The fear of the women at the tomb or of the crowd before Jesus is not a flaw, but the right reaction to the mystery of God. And the exhortation "Do not be afraid" tells us that fear must give way to faith and trust in God.

sens: Struck with surprise and admiration at the sight of an extraordinary event
Overwhelmed by the display of a supernatural power
G1569.detail:
1. The word describes the state of a person seized by surprise at a remarkable fact. It is a astonishment mixed with admiration: the people in Jerusalem see Peter and John heal a lame man and cannot take their eyes off this miracle (Acts 3:11).
2. This surprise is not ordinary: it arises from the spectacle of a power that exceeds the normal, the divine power manifested. The word carries the idea of an almost paralyzing astonishment in the face of the extraordinary.
G1569.origine: The word comes from the Greek preposition « ek » (out of, outside) combined with « thambos » (astonishment, fear). The image is that of a shock that takes you out of yourself, that deeply disturbs you. It is a word that reinforces the idea of surprise by adding the intensity of emotional shock. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament used similar roots to express terror or dread in the face of God's works.
G1569.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 3:11. It describes the reaction of the people who, seeing the lame man now healed and walking beside Peter and John, are seized with admiring astonishment. The context is that of the first miracles of the Church after Pentecost: the power of Christ in action provokes not only surprise among the eyewitnesses but also a wonder that paralyzes and draws them in. The people cannot help but rush over.
G1569.portee: This word reminds us that the works of God always produce a profound impression on those who see them sincerely. The healing of the lame man was not just a curiosity among others, but a sign of the power of the Resurrected One. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation not to remain indifferent to the manifestations of God's power: they should seize us and lead us to seek Him, just as the people approached.

sens: Abandon a child to die or be taken in
Reject, put outside
G1570.detail:
1. To expose a child means to abandon them by leaving them outside, unprotected, in the hope that they will die or that someone will take them in. It is an act of brutal rejection that reveals the hard heart of a society. In Acts 7:19, Stephen recalls how the Egyptian pharaoh forced the Hebrews to "expose" their newborn children, depriving them of life and paternal protection — a cruelty aimed at destroying the people of Israel.
2. In a broader figurative sense, the word can mean to reject or cast aside something or someone, to put them outside as undesirable or worthless.
G1570.origine: The Greek word « ekthetos » comes from the preposition « ek » (out of) and the verb « tithemi » (to place, to put). The basic image is that of something put outside, thrown out. It is a compound word that describes the action of highlighting by rejection. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates Hebrew expressions describing the abandonment of a child.
G1570.emploi: The word « ekthetos » appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:19. It is Stephen who uses it in his final speech before the Sanhedrin to describe the cruelty of the pharaoh towards the Hebrew children. The context is that of persecution: the recounting of this ancient crime illustrates how God has always had a persecuted people. The use of the word emphasizes the terrible reality and barbarity of this practice in the ancient world.
G1570.portee: This word confronts the reader with an inhumane reality: the abandonment of innocent children. By recalling this, Stephen shows that God sees the hidden sufferings and secret crimes of humanity, even the oldest ones. For the Christian, it is a call to defend fragile life and to recognize that God protects the weak and the abandoned.

sens: Remove completely an impurity, clean thoroughly
Eliminate what corrupts or defiles
Keep oneself pure by staying away from what is evil
G1571.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to clean, to remove entirely": it is a complete and radical cleaning. In 1 Corinthians 5:7, Paul commands the Corinthians to "purge out the old leaven" from their community, just as one clears a house of leaven before Passover, because leaven symbolizes sin that spoils the whole batch.
2. In a moral and spiritual sense, to purify means "to remove evil". It is the image of leaven that ferments and contaminates: it must be eliminated radically, without allowing it to work.
3. For a believer, to purify oneself is to "keep oneself pure" by voluntarily abstaining from what defiles (2 Timothy 2:21). It is an active choice: one refuses what is impure to remain clean before God and useful for His works.
G1571.origine: The Greek word combines « ek » (out, outside) and « kathairō » (to clean, to purify): the idea is to "cast out" everything that is impure. It is a reinforcement of the simple action of purifying. In Hebrew, the underlying word is often « bâ'ar » (to sweep away, to carry off), which has the same sense of radical cleaning and elimination.
G1571.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, always to express a radical and urgent purification. In 1 Corinthians 5:7, it concerns the entire community: Paul asks the Corinthians to remove the leaven of sin, just as one prepares for Passover. In 2 Timothy 2:21, it is about a personal decision: the believer who keeps himself pure becomes an honorable instrument in the hands of the Lord. In both cases, the purification is moral and spiritual, not physical, and it requires a deliberate action.
G1571.portee: This word calls the believer to a clear break with sin. It is not about gradual improvement, but total elimination. Purity is not passive: it is a choice to refuse what corrupts and to actively distance oneself from it. A purified believer becomes useful to the Lord for His works, hence the importance of this radicality.

sens: Burn, be consumed by fire
Flare up, light up intensely
Be dominated by a passion, a burning desire
G1572.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word describes a fire that awakens and consumes: something ignites, burns with intense heat. It is the image of combustion, of something that lights up suddenly.
2. From there, it also designates the moment when one "catches fire": to ignite means to move from a calm state to a burning, fiery state. The intensity rises suddenly.
3. Applied to emotions and desires, it depicts a person overwhelmed by a passion that burns them from within. In Romans 1:27, men "ignite" in disordered desires: it is the passion that consumes them, that reigns over them, that completely dominates them. The inner fire of desires masters them.
G1572.origine: The word is formed from the preposition ἐκ (« out of, from ») and the verb καίω (« to burn »). The idea is that of a combustion that emerges, that explodes. In Hebrew, the word בָּעַר (« to burn ») expressed the same image of fire that consumes. The family of the word includes other verbs of burning and inflaming, all built on this central image of fire.
G1572.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 1:27, regarding disordered passions. Paul uses it to describe how men, having rejected God, are given over to desires contrary to nature — and these desires dominate them, "ignite" them completely. It is a strong word that shows the destructive intensity of covetousness: it not only controls, it burns, it consumes. The image of fire underscores the violent and overwhelming nature of this passion.
G1572.portee: This word reminds the reader that disordered passions are not mere fleeting thoughts: they burn, they consume, they completely master those who nurture them. In reading this, one understands that yielding to desires contrary to God's nature is to allow oneself to be devoured by an inner fire. It is an invitation not to let desires consume us, but to seek freedom in Christ.

sens: To cease to have courage, confidence, or energy in the face of difficulty
To give up effort, to slacken in an undertaken action
To weaken morally, to become discouraged under the weight of trials
G1573.detail:
1. Losing heart means feeling one's heart weaken in the face of a difficult task or obstacle. The Greek word combines the idea of coming out of oneself ("ek") and moral weakness ("kakos", evil). It is the opposite of perseverance: one gives up internally before even failing externally. In 2 Corinthians 4:1, Paul states, "we do not lose heart" despite the trials of apostolic ministry.
2. Giving up effort means gradually slacking off in an action that has been started, letting one's arms drop. The parable in Luke 18:1 encourages us to pray "and not lose heart": it is about not allowing fatigue or discouragement to make us cease our prayer, even when the answer is delayed. In Galatians 6:9, Paul says, "let us not grow weary of doing good": to continue acting generously despite fatigue.
3. Weakening morally under the weight of tribulations means that the heart withers in the face of suffering or opposition. In Ephesians 3:13, Paul asks the Ephesians not to lose heart because of his tribulations: he fears that the sight of his chains might discourage them in their faith.
G1573.origine: The Greek word comes from "en" or "ek" (to come out of, out of) and "kakos" (bad, cowardly, morally weak). The basic image is of "coming out of good", straying from it. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates Hebrew expressions that express weariness or moral discouragement (as in Genesis 27:46, where Rebekah says she is "weary" of life).
G1573.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, always in apostolic epistles from the first century. It is used in two main contexts: first in persevering prayer (Luke 18:1), and then in daily Christian life and perseverance in doing good (2 Corinthians 4:1 and 4:16, Galatians 6:9, Ephesians 3:13, 2 Thessalonians 3:13). Paul regularly uses it to exhort the churches not to lose confidence despite external trials (apostolic, persecutions) or spiritual fatigue. The meaning remains constant: it is always a moral weakness, not physical.
G1573.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the Christian in moments of spiritual fatigue. It reminds us that discouragement is a real temptation, one that even the apostles had to fight against. It invites us to recognize that persevering in prayer, in doing good, and in faith despite obstacles is not an option, but an imperative. Finally, it encourages: if Paul exhorts us not to lose heart, it is because God will give the strength to continue.

sens: To pierce the skin or fabric with a sharp point
To seriously wound by thrusting a sharp weapon
Figuratively: to cause deep moral suffering
G1574.detail: 1. The primary meaning is literal: to pierce, to thrust something sharp through an obstacle or body. It is the act of piercing with a spear or sword, which leaves a wound. 2. By extension, the word denotes the act of wounding or killing with a sharp weapon — a brutal and definitive action. 3. In the biblical context, "pierce" takes on a moral and spiritual dimension: it is not only to injure the body but also to reach the heart, causing deep pain. When Scripture says, "They will look on him whom they have pierced" (John 19:37, Revelation 1:7), it refers to the concrete act of soldiers who thrust a spear into Christ's side, but also to the guilt and repentance that this act provokes in the hearts of those who will see the risen Lord.
G1574.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb κεντέω (kenteō), "to prick, to pierce", prefixed by ἐκ (ek), "out of, through" — hence the meaning of "to completely pierce through". The root evokes the image of a point sinking in. The Hebrew verb דָּקַר (daqar), which Greek often translates in the Septuagint, carries the same idea of piercing or transfixing a victim, particularly in a context of armed violence.
G1574.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In John 19:37, it refers to the historical and literal act: a soldier pierced Jesus' side with a spear. In Revelation 1:7, the same word is used to say that everyone "will see him whom they have pierced", meaning they will recognize Christ at his return by the mark of this salvific wound. The context shifts from the past physical act to its eternal significance: those who pierced the Lord will finally understand who he was, and those who see him now will behold the fulfillment of this prophecy.
G1574.portee: This word reminds us that the death of Christ is not a theological abstraction, but a violent and concrete event: he was wounded, pierced for our salvation. It also invites meditation on guilt and grace: those who "pierced" the Lord are confronted with what they have done, but the context of John 19:37 and Revelation 1:7 reveals that this wound is the very heart of salvation and repentance. In contemplating him whom they have pierced, one can only be transformed.

sens: To cut and remove a part of something
Figuratively: to exclude someone from a community or blessing
G1575.detail:
1. The word depicts the action of cutting and removing a part from a whole — like cutting off a branch from a tree. It is concrete, brutal, and definitive. In Romans 11:17, Paul speaks of branches of the olive tree that are "cut off": they are severed and thrown away, separated from the tree that nourished them.
2. Figuratively, to cut off means to exclude, to deprive of the place or blessing one had. The cut-off branches represent the unbelieving Israelites deprived of God's promises. The word does not merely say that they are distant: it emphasizes that they are separated by a definitive divine act, due to their unbelief (Romans 11:20).
G1575.origine: The Greek word is composed of the prefix "ek" (out of) and "klaō" (to break, to shatter). This image of rupture expresses a clear separation. In Hebrew, the verb "shaïa'" (to split, to break) carries the same force of violence and division.
G1575.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Greek Bible, all in Romans 11:17-20. Paul uses it in his great allegory of the olive tree to describe the fate of the natural branches of Israel. They are cut off not by accident or whim, but "because of unbelief" (11:20). This cutting off contrasts with the grafting of the believing Gentile: where there was exclusion, there is now inclusion. The verb thus emphasizes the serious and motivated nature of divine exclusion.
G1575.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God's blessing is never a guaranteed possession, but a gift conditioned by faith. Unbelief can lead to exclusion, like those cut-off branches. At the same time, it invites the believer to humility: the fact that "natural" branches could be cut off shows that no position is unassailable if one abandons trust in God.

sens: Close the door to someone, reject them
Separate someone from a group, remove them
Prohibit, prevent
G1576.detail:
1. The concrete and primary meaning is to completely close off, to bar access. In Romans 3:27, Paul asks: "Where then is the boasting? It is excluded" — literally shut out, forbidden entry. One thinks of a door closed in someone's face.
2. The word can also mean to separate someone from a group or community, to remove them. In Galatians 4:17, some want to "alienate" the Galatians from Paul, that is, to tear them away from his company and influence.
3. The meaning extends to prohibiting, preventing someone from enjoying a right or position. When the Gospel is preached to us, the "law of works" is excluded: it can no longer be our means of salvation and pride before God.
G1576.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐκ ("out of") and κλείω ("to close"). It is a stacking of images: one closes (κλείω), and closes in such a way as to put outside (ἐκ). The root κλείω also appears in κλειστός ("closed") and κλείς ("key"). In the Greek of the Old Testament, it is encountered to express the idea of removing or diverting.
G1576.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two provided passages. In Romans 3:27 (passive form), it is the "law of works" that is excluded from the realm of salvation and glory before God: thanks to the Gospel, one can no longer boast by works.
