In Galatians 4:17 (active form), it is the false apostles who want to "alienate" Christians from Paul — to remove them from his influence to win them over to themselves. In both cases, it is a voluntary and decisive exclusion.
G1576.portee: For the Christian reader, this word illuminates two essential truths: first, that salvation by faith alone excludes any claim to glory through our own works — this is one of Paul's great affirmations. Secondly, that there exists a true and a false community of influence around us, and that some seek to "alienate" us from the truth to distance us from the Lord. The word invites us to stand firm.

sens: Assembly of citizens officially convened
Assembly or community of the people of Israel in the Old Testament
Gathering of Christians for worship
Local community of believers in a place
Entire body of Christians, the universal Church
G1577.detail:
1. In the Greek world, this word designates an assembly of citizens regularly convened for public affairs (Acts 19:32, 39, 40 shows the crowd in Ephesus being called to the assembly).

2. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew word that names the assembly of Israel gathered before God (Acts 7:38 refers to the assembly in the wilderness, during the Law).

3. In the New Testament, it first refers to a group of Christians who gather to pray, learn, and share the Word (1 Corinthians 14:34, 35 regulates the proceedings of these worship assemblies).

4. It is also a community of believers attached to a place: "the church of Jerusalem," "the church that is in their house" (Acts 8:1, 3 speaks of the churches in Judea; Romans 16:5 mentions a church gathered at the home of Priscilla and Aquila).

5. Finally, it is the entirety of all the faithful of Christ throughout time and space, His living body (Matthew 16:18: "I will build my church"; Ephesians 1:22 presents it as the body of Christ).

6. The term also designates a house-church, that is, a small group of believers meeting regularly at one of their homes to live out their faith (Colossians 4:15 speaks of the church at Laodicea).
G1577.origine: The Greek word comes from "to call out" (ἐκ-, "out of," and καλέω, "to call"). Originally, it refers to an assembly of citizens called to meet. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses it to translate the Hebrew word קָהָל which means "assembly, community." In the New Testament, this term inherits this dual meaning: it retains the idea of a public convocation but applies it to the community of believers in Jesus, now the people of God.
G1577.emploi: The word appears 113 times in the New Testament. At first (Acts 5:11), the "assembly" is the entirety of the believers in Jerusalem. Very quickly, the term designates each local community: "the church of Jerusalem," "the church in Corinth" (Acts 8:1; 1 Corinthians 1:2). Paul uses the singular to speak of the local Church where he works (Acts 15:41: "strengthening the churches"), but also the plural to show how several churches support each other (Romans 16:4: "all the churches of the Gentiles"). The letter to the Ephesians elevates the view: the church becomes the body of Christ, a cosmic and eternal reality (Ephesians 1:22; 5:25-27). The term thus encompasses: a one-time act of worship (1 Corinthians 14:34), a lasting local community (Acts 8:3), churches in communion (2 Corinthians 8:24), and the universal Church of the redeemed (Revelation 2:11).
G1577.portee: For the believer, this word roots their faith in a concrete and living reality. The church is not primarily a building, but a people: those whom God has called to leave their occupations to follow Him. It is both the local gathering where we pray and encourage each other (1 Corinthians 14), and the body of Christ without borders or end (Ephesians 1:22). Understanding this word is to discover oneself as a member of a called community, rooted in the promise made to Israel, and destined for eternity with Christ.

sens: To turn away, to stray from the path
To abandon righteousness, to deviate from justice
To flee from evil, to keep away from it
To keep a distance from harmful people
G1578.detail:
1. The word literally evokes the action of turning aside, of straying: it is like leaving a road. In Romans 3:12, it describes how all have turned away from the right path of justice.
2. In the same verse, the meaning broadens to the abandonment of moral uprightness: not following the good, that is, voluntarily straying from what is just.
3. In 1 Peter 3:11, it is precisely "to turn away from evil": the idea is not passive, but active — fleeing sin as one would avoid danger.
4. In Romans 16:17, Paul asks believers to turn away from certain people, those who cause divisions and scandals: it is to stray from a bad influence to protect oneself.
G1578.origine: The word is composed of the prefix ἐκ ("out of") and the verb κλίνω ("to lean, incline"). The basic image is that of one who leans, bends, and turns away — literally, he strays from a direction. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew נָטָה ("to turn, to stray") and סוּר ("to depart"), words that also carry the idea of leaving a path or state.
G1578.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in a moral or spiritual sense, never physical. In Romans 3:12, it describes the universal condition of the sinner: all have turned away from good. In 1 Peter 3:11, it positively invites the believer to flee from evil. In Romans 16:17, Paul uses it as a practical call: to concretely turn away from troublemakers. The meaning remains constant: it is a voluntary turning away, a conscious break with a direction or influence.
G1578.portee: This word reminds the Christian that it is not enough to seek the good: one must also actively turn away from evil and those who teach it. It is a call to real vigilance, not just good intentions, for turning away from evil is a decision that must be made concretely.

sens: to save oneself by swimming away from a place
to escape danger by reaching the water
G1579.detail:
1. The word describes the action of swimming to distance oneself from a location, particularly from a ship or a ship in peril. It is a movement of escape by water: one swims out, one leaves by swimming. In Acts 27:42, during the shipwreck of Paul's vessel, the soldiers discuss killing the prisoners so that none "escape by swimming" to the shore.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of fleeing from danger, of securing oneself by one's own efforts. It is a gesture of survival and autonomy in the face of immediate threat.
G1579.origine: The word combines two elements: the preposition "ek" (out of, outside) and the verb "kolumbaō" (to swim). This composition creates the idea of swimming outward, of moving away by swimming. The Greek verb "kolumbaō" evokes the simple action of swimming. By adding the prefix "ek", it emphasizes the movement of escape, of exit.
G1579.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 27:42, during the shipwreck of the boat carrying Paul to Rome. The Roman soldiers discuss their plan to prevent the prisoners from escaping, and they mention the risk that someone "might escape by swimming." This context of maritime disaster makes the term very concrete: it is a real threat in a survival situation.
G1579.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible is concerned with concrete life scenes and real dangers. The account of the shipwreck in Acts 27 also shows how God protects Paul in the midst of adversity, transforming the soldiers' panic into an opportunity for trust in His providence.

sens: to transport a body outside for burial
to accompany a dead person to their final resting place
G1580.detail:
1. The word describes the action of transporting a body out of a dwelling or city for burial. In Luke 7:12, Jesus encounters a funeral procession that "was carrying" a deceased young man — this refers to the solemn moment when the body, placed on a stretcher, is taken away to be buried according to Jewish customs. It is both a practical and ritually significant act.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes the respect paid to the deceased and the communal accompaniment in death: it is not a simple evacuation, but a procession of mourners and loved ones honoring the dead by carrying them to their tomb.
G1580.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "ek" (out of, outside) and the verb "komizô" (to transport, to carry with care). This composition emphasizes the idea of carrying something outside. The verb "komizô" likely comes from a root denoting the careful transport of a precious object. The preposition "ek" intensifies the idea of direction outward, which in a funeral context acquires particular solemnity.
G1580.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 7:12. It is during the miracle of Nain: Jesus arrives at the city gate just as they "were carrying" out a dead man, a young man who was the only son of a widow. This precise context — a solitary, grieving woman — gives the word its full emotional weight. Jesus is moved with compassion and raises this young man. The verb thus marks the critical moment when death seems definitive: it is when the body is taken out for burial that the impossibility seems total, and it is here that God intervenes.
G1580.portee: This word invites the reader to measure the reality and solemnity of death in the light of faith. It is in this moment of carrying to the tomb — a moment of acceptance and farewell — that Jesus manifests His power over death and His compassion for the grieving. For the Christian, it is a call to hope beyond the grave and to recognize that Jesus alone can transform a situation of mourning into joy.

sens: to slice, separate a part of a body or plant
to remove, eliminate, cut off someone or something
to take away, remove an opportunity, a possibility
G1581.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to sharply slice off a part of a living being. Jesus speaks of cutting off a hand or foot if it leads us to sin (Matthew 5:30; 18:8). It is a radical image of renouncing sinful desires.
2. To apply to a tree or plant: to fell it, eliminate it because it does not bear fruit (Matthew 3:10; Luke 13:7: "Cut it down"). John the Baptist announces that every barren tree will be "cut down" and thrown into the fire; likewise, the vineyard owner orders that the unproductive fig tree be cut down.
3. Figuratively, to take away, cut off an opportunity or possibility: Paul says he cuts off the opportunity (ἀφορμή, the opportunity) for those who want to boast about him (2 Corinthians 11:12). It is an action that deprives someone of a resource or a pretext.
G1581.origine: The word is composed of ἐκ (ek: "out of, outside") and κόπτω (koptō: "to cut, to strike"). This root κόπτω evokes the action of striking, especially with a sharp tool. The word often translates the Hebrew כָּרַת (karat: "to cut, to cut off"), which refers both to the felling of a tree and the breaking of a covenant. The addition of the prefix ἐκ reinforces the idea of complete separation, of definitive cutting off.
G1581.emploi: The verb ἐκκόπτω appears ten times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Luke. Jesus uses it to speak of moral amputation (Matthew 5:30; 18:8): it is not a literal prescription for self-mutilation, but an exhortation to radically eliminate what diverts us from God. John the Baptist and Jesus also use it for the image of the barren tree (Matthew 3:10; 7:19; Luke 3:9; 13:7): a tree that does not bear good fruit must be cut down. Paul uses it figuratively in Romans 11 (to remove an advantage, or cut off a branch from the olive tree) and in 2 Corinthians 11:12 to say that he removes an opportunity from his opponents.
G1581.portee: This word highlights the spiritual urgency: one must act without hesitation against what distances us from God and justice. It also shows that our usefulness before God depends on our spiritual fruitfulness — our works, our fruit. Finally, it reminds us that God's mercy has a limit: persistently rejecting His call exposes one to definitive elimination.

sens: to be hung or attached to something (physical image)
to be completely captivated by someone, hanging on their words or actions
G1582.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word designates the act of being suspended, attached, or hung to something, like hanging an object on a nail. This is the primary image of the Greek word, which combines "out of" and "to hang."
2. In a figurative sense, it means to be completely absorbed, captivated by someone — to be literally "suspended" to their words or actions. In Luke 19:48, the crowd was hanging on Jesus as they listened: they could not detach their attention from him, they were entirely captivated.
G1582.origine: The word comes from the prefix "ek" (out of, from) and the verb "kremao" (to hang, to suspend). This composition creates the idea of hanging from or at a fixed point — hence the image of something that is suspended, that depends on a support. The image evokes dependence: an object hanging on a nail entirely depends on the nail for support; similarly, someone "suspended" to the words of a speaker depends on them for their attention and interest.
G1582.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 19:48, during the last week of Jesus in Jerusalem. Luke recounts that the chief priests and the scribes sought to kill Jesus, but they did not know how to do it. Why? Because "all the people were listening to him with admiration" — literally, they were hanging on him. It is in this context of tension that the word resonates: despite the murderous intentions of the authorities, they remained paralyzed by the hold that Jesus had over the crowd.
G1582.portee: This word shows how Jesus captivated people's attention, not by force, but by the power of His word. For the reader, it invites recognition of this attraction that Jesus' teaching exerts — a fascination that comes from the authority and grace of His presence. It also questions the believer: are we "suspended" to His words with that same complete attention?

sens: To report orally, to make known by word
To disclose, reveal what should remain secret
G1583.detail:
1. To report orally, to make known by word: this means to convey information, news, or a message to someone by directly telling them. In Acts 23:22, the tribune asks the young man to "speak" about the report he received — that is, not to disclose the details of the conspiracy he has just confided to the commander.
2. To disclose, reveal what should remain secret: the word emphasizes the confidential or dangerous nature of what is communicated. Here, the tribune fears that if the young man "speaks" of his denunciation, the conspirators will learn of it and kill him; he therefore orders him to remain silent.
G1583.origine: The word is composed of ἐκ ("out of," "outside") and λαλέω ("to speak"). Literally, it means "to speak out" or "to let out by word." This image evokes the action of making known outside what was hidden, letting escape by the mouth what one should have kept to oneself. The verb λαλέω is very common in the New Testament in the sense of "to speak," "to say."
G1583.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:22. The scene recounts how Paul is arrested in Jerusalem and imprisoned. A young man learns of a conspiracy: Jews have formed a plot to kill Paul. This young man will report the threat to the Roman tribune. To protect the young man and his secret, the tribune formally orders him not to "speak" to anyone about the "report" he has confided to him. The context shows that "to speak of" here means "to disclose" or "to report" dangerous information.
G1583.portee: This word shows us the importance of secrecy and caution in perilous situations. The tribune protects the young man by forbidding him to speak — not out of malice, but to preserve him from danger. This reminds us that sometimes, keeping silent is not dishonesty, but a form of wisdom and protection for others.

sens: To shine intensely, like a light that bursts forth
To radiate brilliance and splendor
To be remarkable, striking by excellence
G1584.detail:
1. The verb describes a light that comes forth vividly, bursting outward. The image is that of the sun shining in all its brightness: in Matthew 13:43, the righteous "will shine like the sun" — they will shine with an intense and visible clarity.
2. The meaning extends to any glorious radiance: to shine is to manifest a beauty or a dazzling splendor that attracts attention. It is glory brought to light.
3. By extension, it also means to shine by some moral or spiritual excellence: to stand out, to be remarkable for one's virtue or status. The righteous in the kingdom shine not only physically but by their restored excellence.
G1584.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "ek" (out, outside) and the verb "lampō" (to shine, to glow). This combination suggests a light that comes forth, bursting outward — a brightness that expresses itself clearly. The root "lampō" is connected to biblical images of divine radiance: the glory of God appearing, becoming visible. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb could translate the Hebrew word meaning "to illuminate" or "to shine forth."
G1584.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Matthew 13:43, at the end of the parable of the wheat and the tares. Jesus describes the moment of final judgment, when the righteous will shine in the kingdom of their Father. The context is eschatological: it is a promise concerning the future glory of the faithful. The word is used only for this vision of the coming reign of God, which underscores its sublime character and its direct link to the transformation and final glorification of the elect.
G1584.portee: For the Christian, this verb inspires hope. It reminds us that justice and faithfulness do not remain hidden or diminished: they will one day be manifested in full glory. It is a word of comfort for those who suffer in silence or who are unknown on earth. It also affirms that eternal life is not a dull existence: it will be radiant, shining, filled with a visible glory that reflects that of Christ himself.

sens: To cease to remember something, to lose it from mind
To set aside, to intentionally neglect or overlook
To not take into account, to deliberately ignore
G1585.detail:
1. To completely forget means to let something that should have been retained slip out of one's mind. It is stronger than a mere passing forgetfulness: it is a total loss of memory. When the Hebrews "forget" the Lord's exhortation (Hebrews 12:5), they no longer remember the words of correction He addresses to them.

2. This verb can also refer to neglecting or setting aside something important. It is less about the memory fading than the attention one gives to it. To forget the Lord's exhortation is also to refuse to listen to it, to take it seriously.

3. In its strongest usage, to forget means to deliberately ignore, to act as if something does not exist. The word suggests a certain willfulness: one chooses not to take into account what should guide us.
G1585.origine: The Greek word ἐκλανθάνω is composed of the prefix ἐκ (ek, "out of") and the verb λανθάνω (lanthanō, "to escape attention, to be hidden"). This composition reinforces the idea: the forgetfulness is complete, radical, as if the thing has entirely escaped the mind. The simple verb λανθάνω means primarily "to go unnoticed" or "to escape notice"; with the prefix, it becomes "to totally escape memory." It is a word that emphasizes the depth and completeness of forgetfulness.
G1585.emploi: This verb appears only once in the preserved New Testament, in Hebrews 12:5. The author of the epistle exhorts the Hebrews not to forget the word of encouragement that God addresses to them through Proverbs (3:11-12), inviting the people to see divine discipline not as abandonment, but as a mark of paternal love. Not to "forget" this exhortation means to remain attentive to it, to keep it alive in the heart despite trials. The context shows that it is less about a simple memory lapse than about spiritual negligence: one must remember that God corrects those He loves.
G1585.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us of the importance of constantly keeping the word of God before us, especially in times of suffering or discipline. To forget what God tells us is to risk losing the sense of His correction and love. It is a call to spiritual vigilance: to keep in mind that every trial is a word from the Father educating us.

sens: Select someone or something from others for oneself
Designate someone for a role or responsibility
Prefer one option over another in a voluntary act
Elect or distinguish by a divine act of grace
Have been chosen, be among the chosen
G1586.detail:
1. The most basic meaning is to take, to select: one chooses from several possibilities. Mary "chose the good part" by sitting at Jesus' feet (Luke 10:42), she preferred this option over that of her sister. It is an act of personal and conscious decision.

2. When one chooses someone for a position or mission, one designates them for that. The apostles "thought it best to choose delegates" (Acts 15:25) to send to the other churches: it is an appointment for a role.

3. On a human scale, the word retains its weight: when Jesus "chose" his twelve apostles (Luke 6:13), he made a deliberate selection among his disciples. It is an act of clear will.

4. But the Bible also uses this word for God's decision regarding the people or believers. God "chose our fathers" of Israel (Acts 13:17), setting them apart for Himself. It is a choice of grace, a divine election that establishes the relationship with God. Ephesians 1:4 confirms this: it is the work of the Father who chooses His own.

5. The word also designates the state of one who is chosen: being among the "elect" means bearing the mark of this divine selection (Mark 13:20). It is an identity and a promise.
G1586.origine: The Greek word combines "ek" (out of, from) and "legō" (to gather, to collect) — the image is that of selecting from outside, by sorting. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew "bachar," which means "to sort, to choose, to examine." In Hebrew as well, divine choice is a sorting, a setting apart for a covenant: this is why "elect" and "chosen" are almost synonymous in biblical theology. The word carries the idea of intentional discrimination, of sorting according to judgment.
G1586.emploi: The word appears about 20 times in the New Testament. It is first used in ordinary human choices: choosing a portion of food (Luke 10:42), designating delegates (Acts 15:25). But it is mainly used for divine decisions or those of Jesus. Jesus "chose" his apostles, not arbitrarily, but according to His will (Luke 6:13, John 13:18). The recurring idea is that this choice confers an identity and a responsibility: one is "chosen" for a mission. The word is also used for God's choice within the history of salvation: He chose Israel (Acts 13:17), then He chooses believers in Christ (Ephesians 1:4). Even in texts where divine election occurs, the choice does not negate consciousness or discernment: it is an act of intelligent will, not a blind mechanism.
G1586.portee: This word reminds us that in spiritual life, choice is never neutral: choosing Christ, choosing the will of God, means setting oneself apart, entering into a destiny. It also sheds light on the mystery of grace: God "chooses" us, not because we are better than others, but out of pure mercy. It is a word of comfort for the believer: our relationship with God is not the result of chance, but of an election. It also invites moral vigilance: one who is "chosen" to follow Jesus receives a calling, not an exemption.

sens: Cease to be present, disappear
Come to an end, take finish
Fail, abandon someone
G1587.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: unjust riches can fail, that is, disappear or be exhausted (Luke 16:9). The word evokes something that goes away, that is no longer there.
2. Come to an end, like the years of the Lord that will never end (Hebrews 1:12), or like the sunlight that darkens during an eclipse (Luke 23:45). It is the idea that something reaches its term.
3. In a more personal sense: a virtue, a strength, or a faithfulness can fail. Peter's faith must not fail at the moment of trials (Luke 22:32) — here the word denotes the abandonment or exhaustion of an inner strength.
G1587.origine: The word comes from the prefix "ek" (out of, outside) and the verb "leipo" (to leave, to quit). The basic image is therefore "to leave aside" or "to go out of." In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates several Hebrew verbs that express the idea of completion, disappearance, or rupture.
G1587.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in Luke and in the epistle to the Hebrews. In Luke 16:9, it describes how riches are exhausted or disappear. In Luke 22:32, applied to faith, it means a possible failure or cessation of trust. In Luke 23:45, it describes the darkening of the sun — a physical phenomenon of eclipse. In Hebrews 1:12, it denotes the absence of end, affirming that God's years will never end. The word thus covers both the physical, temporal, and spiritual domains.
G1587.portee: This word reminds the Christian of the fragility of all that is earthly — money, human strength, even the light of the sun can disappear. But conversely, it affirms the permanence of God and His faithfulness, which knows neither wear nor failure. It is a call to place one's trust not in what can fail, but in the eternal God.

sens: Chosen, selected from others for quality or excellence
One whom God has chosen for Himself, recipient of His favor
Christ, precious stone chosen by God as foundation
The angels chosen by God
The Christians chosen by God before the foundation of the world
G1588.detail:
1. In its primary sense, the word designates what is chosen, selected for its exceptional qualities — as one chooses the best pieces at a market. Romans 16:13 speaks of a remarkable person "in the Lord."
2. In the Bible, especially from the Old Testament onward, this word takes on a spiritual dimension: it refers to those whom God has chosen, whom God calls "His own." Luke 18:7 mentions the "elect" who cry out to God.
3. Jesus Himself is the elect par excellence: 1 Peter 2:4-6 designates Him as the "precious stone, chosen" upon which the people of God is built.
4. The angels are said to be elect: 1 Timothy 5:21 speaks of the "elect angels," those whom God has set apart for His service.
5. Christians are the elect of God. Matthew 22:14 distinguishes the "called" (all those who hear the invitation) from the "elect" (those who truly respond). Colossians 3:12 addresses Christians as the "elect of God," marking that they were chosen even before the foundation of the world.
G1588.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to gather," "to choose." In classical Greek, it simply designates the chosen, the selected. In Hebrew, it corresponds to the verb "to choose" (bâchar) which often appears in the Old Testament to describe God's sovereign choice: He chooses Abraham, Israel, kings, worthy sacrifices. This is not a choice based on merit, but on God's free and sovereign will.
G1588.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Luke to speak of Jesus and those who belong to Him. Matthew 24:22, 24, 31 uses it for the disciples gathered in the last days. Romans 8:33 uses the expression "elect of God" to affirm that nothing can accuse them before God. 1 Peter 1:1; 2:9 speaks of Christians as a "chosen people." Revelation 17:14 qualifies those who follow the Lamb as "called, chosen, and faithful." The meaning remains constant: these are those whom God has set apart for Himself, not by chance, but by deliberate choice.
G1588.portee: For the believer, this word reminds that his relationship with God is not the result of chance or his own effort alone: God has chosen him. This is a source of confidence and humility: confidence that God will not abandon him (Romans 8:33), humility in the face of the privilege received without having earned it. It is also a call to faithfulness — being chosen requires a response, a sanctification.

sens: The action of choosing someone or something
God's choice to select certain people for a specific mission or salvation
The condition of one who is chosen by God
The group of people that God has chosen
G1589.detail:
1. In its primary sense, the word refers to the action of choosing: it is the act of designating someone among others. In Acts 9:15, Paul is called "an instrument" of election, meaning that God has specifically chosen him for a task.

2. In the New Testament, this word always speaks of God's choice regarding His people or His servants, not a mere human preference. Romans 9:11 explains that this choice of God exists "without depending on works," meaning that God elects even before anyone has done good or evil.

3. The word can also refer to the state of one who has been elected: being under God's election means having been personally chosen by Him. In 1 Thessalonians 1:4, the apostle affirms that believers have "been elected": they are in this state of being chosen.

4. By extension, "election" can refer to the entire group of those whom God has chosen: in Romans 11:7, "the election" takes on the meaning of "the elect" — it is the community of those whom God selects for salvation.
G1589.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "eklegō" which means "to choose out" or "to select." It is composed of the prefix "ek" (out of) and the verb "legō" (to gather, to choose): the image is that of someone selecting certain things from a whole. In Romans 11:5, Paul speaks of "an election of grace," showing that this choice comes entirely from God's free goodness.
G1589.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the epistles of Paul and Peter. It is used to describe the divine choice that precedes each person's history: God chooses certain individuals (Paul in Acts 9:15) and an entire people (Israel in Romans 11:28) according to His sovereign will, not according to their merits. In Romans 11, Paul argues that even if Israel has rejected the Gospel, God maintains an election according to grace. The word can refer to the action itself (Romans 9:11), the elected person (1 Thessalonians 1:4), or the group of the elect (Romans 11:7).
G1589.portee: This word reveals a central truth of the Christian faith: our salvation does not depend on our efforts or merits, but on God's free choice. It invites the believer to humility before divine sovereignty and to gratitude towards the One who chose him before the foundation of the world. It is also a source of security: being elected by God means that God has destined us for eternity.

sens: To lack physical strength, vigor
To slacken one's effort, become less vigorous
To lack courage, be discouraged in the face of adversity
To weaken internally in the face of a trial
G1590.detail:
1. To lose physical strength or lack the energy to continue: it is the exhaustion of the body. Jesus fears that the crowds following Him for three days without food may collapse from starvation on the way (Matthew 15:32, Mark 8:3).
2. To slacken the effort one is putting forth, to cease holding firm: it is like an archer who lets his bow relax. Paul exhorts the Galatians not to lose heart in doing good (Galatians 6:9).
3. To lose courage in the face of difficulty, to become morally downcast: it is the soul that weakens. The Hebrews are encouraged not to be discouraged by trials (Hebrews 12:3, 12:5).
4. To weaken in perseverance due to a prolonged trial: the inner resistance that gives way. This is the sense that unites all usages: from the exhausted body to the wavering will.
G1590.origine: The word comes from ἐκ ("out, away") and λύω ("to loosen, to relax"). The basic image is that of a rope being loosened, of a bow being relaxed. Starting from this physical sense (losing tension, rigidity), the word glides towards moral meaning: to slacken one's moral effort, courage, vigilance. It is a typically Greek compound verb that combines the idea of going out/removing (ἐκ) with that of undoing (λύω) to express a weakening.
G1590.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament. Two usages concern direct physical exhaustion: the crowds following Jesus risk losing strength (Matthew 15:32, Mark 8:3). The other three usages, in Paul and the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, relate to moral or spiritual exhaustion: not to become weary in doing good (Galatians 6:9), not to be discouraged by opposition or suffering (Hebrews 12:3, 12:5). The context thus broadens the meaning from simple physical weakening to spiritual tenacity, to the persevering courage that the Christian must cultivate.
G1590.portee: This word calls the believer to vigilance on two levels: first, to take care of his body and energy (for the Lord is attentive to our strength), and especially to strengthen his heart in the face of trials. Losing heart is not a shameful weakness, but a risk that the Bible acknowledges—hence the importance of rooting oneself in perseverance, as Paul and the author of Hebrews teach. It is an invitation not to abandon the race, whatever the cost.

sens: To remove moisture, water, or tears from a surface by lightly rubbing it with a cloth or absorbent material
To gently clean a part of another person's body, out of respect or service
To erase or remove something material or figurative
G1591.detail:
1. To wipe means to remove water or moisture by rubbing: Mary wipes the tears she has shed on Jesus' feet with her own hair (Luke 7:38), and Jesus wipes the feet of His disciples with the cloth He is wearing (John 13:5). It is a simple and everyday gesture, but here it becomes an act filled with love.
2. In the Bible, wiping often takes on a dimension of personal service and honor: by wiping someone's feet, one acknowledges their importance and performs an act of devotion. Mary's act of kneeling and wiping the Lord's feet with her hair expresses her repentance and worship (Luke 7:44; John 12:3). Similarly, when Jesus washes and wipes the feet of His disciples, it is a voluntary humiliating gesture that shows radical service.
G1591.origine: The Greek word ἐκμάσσω is composed of ἐκ ("out of, from") and μάσσω ("to rub, to wipe"). It literally means "to rub off." The root evokes the physical action of rubbing or cleaning by friction. This verb always expresses a deliberate act of removing something by rubbing.
G1591.emploi: The verb to wipe appears 5 times in the New Testament, exclusively in Luke and John. Four of these usages concern the remarkable act of Mary wiping Jesus' feet with her hair (Luke 7:38, 44; John 11:2; 12:3): it is an act of feminine devotion and repentance before the Lord. The fifth usage (John 13:5) shows Jesus Himself wiping the feet of His disciples after washing them, reversing social roles and manifesting His love through service. In all cases, the word denotes a personal, humble, and meaningful gesture.
G1591.portee: This word reveals the dignity of humbly offered service, especially when the one serving is in a position of power: Jesus wiping the feet of His disciples teaches us that true power lies in self-giving. Mary's act teaches us that worship and repentance come through visible, personal, and often costly gestures. To wipe is not only to clean, but to honor the one being served.

sens: To hold someone in derision, to mock them with contempt and malice
To ridicule someone in public, to make them a laughingstock before others
G1592.detail:
1. To hold someone in derision, to mock them with contempt and malice: the Greek word ἐκμυκτηρίζω combines the idea of "holding the nose up" (physical contempt) with that of ridicule. It is to manifestly and cruelly despise someone. In Luke 16:14, the Pharisees "mocked" Jesus by rejecting his teaching on money, treating him with disdain.
2. To ridicule someone in public, to make them a laughingstock before others: this mockery is not silent; it is shown, displayed, intended to humiliate the victim in front of witnesses. In Luke 23:35, "the rulers mocked" Jesus on the cross, publicly shouting that if he were really the Christ, he should save himself — an attempt to discredit Jesus before the crowd present.
G1592.origine: The Greek word ἐκμυκτηρίζω comes from the prefix ἐκ ("out of," "from") and the verb μυκτηρίζω, which literally evokes the gesture of wrinkling the nose — the classic gesture of contempt and derision in the Greek world. This image of the nose held high symbolizes disgust and insolence. The word appears in the Greek Old Testament, notably as a translation of the Hebrew verb לָעַג ("to mock"), which has the same nuance of public and humiliating ridicule.
G1592.emploi: The verb ἐκμυκτηρίζω appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Luke: in 16:14 and 23:35. In both cases, it describes hostile and public mockery directed against Jesus. In 16:14, the Pharisees "mock" Jesus because he questions their attachment to money, thus revealing their hearts. In 23:35, the mockery is even more cruel: it occurs during the crucifixion, when Jesus is defenseless and at the mercy of those who ridicule him. In both contexts, the mockery is a deliberate act of contempt, often motivated by religious hostility or malice.
G1592.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that public contempt and mockery are weapons of sin against the truth and against those who proclaim it. Jesus himself was mocked, not out of ignorance, but by conscious malice from those who refused to submit to his word. Understanding this verb is to see how mockery can be a subtle or manifest form of rejection of God and his kingdom.

sens: To discreetly withdraw from a place
To slip away from a group or crowd
To avoid someone by fleeing
G1593.detail:
1. The word evokes the idea of turning away, withdrawing by stepping aside — like someone who lowers their head to slip out of a place unnoticed. In John 5:13, Jesus "disappears" from the crowd after healing the sick man at the pool of Bethesda: he discreetly slips away among the gathered people.
2. It is also the action of avoiding someone or something by retreating, by eluding — not through a sudden absence, but through a deliberate withdrawal. The word suggests discretion, an evasion rather than a noisy escape.
G1593.origine: The word is composed of "ék" (out of, away from) and "néuo" (to incline, to bend, to turn the head). The basic image is that of the head inclining to turn away — the gesture of someone who evades, who withdraws. It is a classical Greek word attested in historians and playwrights.
G1593.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 5:13. There, it describes the moment when Jesus, after healing the infirm man at Bethesda, discreetly withdraws from the crowd. This unique usage emphasizes Jesus' discretion: he does not seek fame or recognition for his miracle. He simply disappears, allowing the healed man to later discover who saved him.
G1593.portee: This word shows how Jesus acts with a certain reserve: he heals but does not expose himself or claim glory. For the reader, it is a reminder that true spiritual power does not cry out for the admiration of the world. Jesus withdraws, and it is then, in silence, that the miracle bears fruit in the life of the healed man.

sens: To sober up, to awaken after being drunk
To regain composure, to find clarity and discernment
To regain one's senses in the face of an error or illusion
G1594.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the act of becoming sober after drunkenness, shaking off the numbness caused by alcohol. It is the image of a person awakening, like Noah in Genesis 9:24 who "came to himself from his drunkenness."
2. Metaphorically, it means to regain clarity and mental insight, to chase away the fog that obscures judgment. In 1 Corinthians 15:34, Paul urges the Corinthians to "come to yourselves": he calls them to regain composure and think clearly.
3. More broadly, the word means to awaken to an illusion, an error, or a seduction, to regain one's senses like someone emerging from troubled sleep. It is to regain moral and spiritual sobriety, the ability to judge soundly.
G1594.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "ek" ("out of," "from among") and "nephō" ("to be sober"). It literally means "to come out of drunkenness." The underlying verb "nephō" is rooted in the idea of mental clarity, of non-intoxication. The fundamental image comes from the contrast between drunkenness that troubles and sobriety that enlightens: the Hebrew word "yaqatz" (יָקַץ), translated by this term in Genesis 9:24 and Habakkuk 2:7, expresses the idea of awakening, of rising after sleep or torpor.
G1594.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 15:34. Paul uses it to address the Corinthians who denied the resurrection of the dead — a serious deviation that showed mental and spiritual confusion. By saying "Come to yourselves" (literally "see from your drunkenness"), Paul exhorts them to abandon this doctrinal error and to regain right judgment, based on the reality of Christ's resurrection. The context shows that this "drunkenness" is not a physical state but a spiritual and moral one.
G1594.portee: This word calls the Christian reader to vigilance and spiritual clarity. It reminds us that false doctrines, sin, and forgetfulness of God can make us "drunk" — unable to see the truth clearly. To come to oneself is to accept being awakened by the word of God and to resort to clear thinking based on the revelation of Christ. It is also a call to urgency: it is time to regain composure before it is too late.

sens: acting of one's own free will, without constraint
arising from a free choice, a personal decision
coming from the heart, without obligation
G1595.detail:
1. The word describes an action, attitude, or gift that comes from the free choice of the one acting, without force or external pressure. It is the opposite of what one would do out of obligation or fear. In Philemon 1:14, Paul wishes that Philemon's service to Onesimus be 'voluntary' — not imposed by the apostle, but freely consented to by Philemon's own heart.
2. The word emphasizes the inner movement: the one who acts voluntarily commits with all their conscience and will. It is an act that reflects what one truly desires to do, not what one is forced to do.
3. In Jewish worship, 'voluntary' offerings — those that each person chose to present beyond the sacrifices imposed by the Law — manifested love and generosity of heart towards God.
G1595.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning 'will' or 'agreement of the will'. In Hebrew, it often translates the word נְדָבָה (nédaba), which refers to gifts or offerings made from the heart, without legal obligation. This Hebrew notion of free offering has profoundly influenced the piety of God's people.
G1595.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Philemon 1:14. Paul uses it to express his desire that Philemon grant his forgiveness and help to Onesimus freely and generously, not compelled by an apostolic letter. It is a delicate pastoral act: the apostle could have commanded, but he prefers that love acts freely. The context shows that Paul values the personal decision inspired by grace, rather than mechanical obedience.
G1595.portee: This word reminds Christians that God desires our heartfelt acts, not our forced obedience. Service, forgiveness, and generosity have true value only if they arise from a free will, animated by the love of Christ. It is a lesson for those in authority: to inspire rather than coerce, so that good springs from a heart transformed by grace.

sens: Of one's own will, without external constraint or obligation
By deliberate and conscious choice of what one is doing
G1596.detail:
1. The word describes an action done of one's own will, without force or obligation compelling it. In 1 Peter 5:2, elders must shepherd the flock of God 'voluntarily' — that is, out of love and personal devotion, not because they are forced. It is the opposite of acting under compulsion.

2. It also emphasizes that one acts knowingly, understanding what one is doing. In Hebrews 10:26, to sin 'voluntarily' after receiving the truth means committing sin with eyes wide open, deliberately refusing to follow what one knows to be right. It is a conscious and responsible choice.
G1596.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἑκών (hekôn), which means 'voluntary' or 'willing'. The -ως (-ōs) ending makes it an adverb: it changes the word into a manner of doing. This root expresses the idea of choosing freely, giving one's assent. It is a common word in classical Greek to describe actions done 'willingly'.
G1596.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Hebrews 10:26, it qualifies the persistent sin after knowledge of the truth — a voluntary refusal to repent. In 1 Peter 5:2, it describes the service of elders in the Church — they must lead the flock not under compulsion, but with free consent and eagerness. In both cases, it denotes a conscious and deliberate act, which makes the responsibility all the greater.
G1596.portee: This word reminds Christians that God values heartfelt service, not forced obedience. For church leaders, it is a call to serve out of true love, not obligation or self-interest. For every believer, it also emphasizes that deliberately rejecting the light of the Gospel is a serious decision — because it is conscious and voluntary.

sens: From a distant time, from antiquity
That has lasted for a very long time, persistently
G1597.detail:
1. The word designates a distant, remote time, that of yesteryear — what has happened 'long ago'. In 2 Peter 3:5, it speaks of the heavens that existed 'of old' by the word of God: this refers to the distant time of creation, that of the world's origins.
2. But the word also evokes a duration that extends from that distant past to the present, a threat or situation that has persisted for a long time. In 2 Peter 2:3, condemnation threatens 'long ago' the false teachers — this means it has been pronounced over them for a long time, that it remains suspended over them.
G1597.origine: The word is composed of two parts: ἔκ- ('ex-', out of, since) and παλαι ('ancient, of old'). It is a characteristic compound adverb of the late Greek of the New Testament period. The word refers to the idea of ancient, bygone, distant time.
G1597.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the second epistle of Peter (2 Peter 2:3 and 3:5). In 2 Peter 2:3, it qualifies the threat of condemnation hanging over false teachers — an ancient threat, inscribed since the beginning. In 2 Peter 3:5, it relates to the very distant time of the creation of the heavens. In both cases, it refers to a stable, established, irrevocable past.
G1597.portee: This word reminds us that God masters time in its entirety — from the most distant past to the present moment. For the reader, this means that God's judgments have been set for a long time and that His creative words have eternal power. It is an invitation to respect the constancy and continuity of the divine plan.

sens: To put to the test, to submit to a test to know the reaction or strength
To seek to make someone fail by pushing them to sin or do evil
To challenge someone, to throw down a challenge by doubting their faithfulness or strength
G1598.detail:
1. To tempt someone primarily means to put them to the test to see how they will react or how they will hold up. It is to try someone as one would test a weapon or a material. In 1 Corinthians 10:9, Paul warns: "Let us not tempt the Lord, as some of them did," speaking of the Israelites who tested God in the wilderness by doubting His faithfulness.
2. However, to tempt also means to seek to make someone fall into sin or to push them to disobey. It is to seduce towards evil. The devil, in the accounts of Matthew 4:7 and Luke 4:12, tempts Jesus in the wilderness by challenging Him to prove that He is the Son of God — he seeks to make Him act selfishly or wickedly.
3. To tempt also implies provocation: to challenge someone by questioning their word or ability. When the lawyer approaches Jesus in Luke 10:25 to "test" Him, he seeks to put Him in a difficult position, to trap Him with a question.
G1598.origine: The word comes from the Greek root πειράζω (peirazō), "to test," preceded by the prefix ἐκ (ek), "out of" or "from," which reinforces the idea of intense or complete testing. In Hebrew, the word נָסָה (nasah), "to tempt" or "to test," expresses the action of submitting someone or something to a test. The Greek ἐκπειράζω appears mainly in passages where Old Testament words about Israel's trials in the wilderness are cited or referenced (Deuteronomy 6:16).
G1598.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in decisive contexts. In Matthew 4:7 and Luke 4:12, Jesus responds to the devil during the temptation in the wilderness by quoting the Old Testament: "You shall not tempt the Lord your God" — the issue is whether one will challenge God or trust Him. In 1 Corinthians 10:9, Paul warns Christians not to tempt the Lord as the Israelites did, for it led to death. In Luke 10:25, a lawyer approaches Jesus to "test" or put Him to the test with questions. The word thus designates both a trial aimed at seducing towards evil (the action of the devil) and a provocation or doubt towards God (the action of men).
G1598.portee: Understanding this word helps the Christian discern two opposing attitudes towards God: one that tempts Him by doubting Him and challenging Him, and one that trusts Him. Jesus teaches that to tempt God is to refuse to believe in His word and faithfulness. For the believer, this invites examination of whether we truly place our trust in God or if we subject Him to our conditions and doubts. The word also shows how sin often arises from provocation: the devil tempts us by pushing us to prove something in a carnal way rather than by faith.

sens: To make someone leave a place for the accomplishment of a mission
To send someone away, to dispatch someone hastily
G1599.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to make someone leave for a task that has been entrusted to them. In Acts 13:4, it is the Holy Spirit Himself who "sends" Barnabas and Saul on a mission: they are deployed as important messengers, tasked with proclaiming the Gospel. The word carries the idea of scope, of an official mission.
2. The second meaning is more urgent: it is to send someone away, to make them leave quickly. In Acts 17:10, the brothers in Thessalonica "send away" Paul and Silas by night, to keep them safe from the hostile crowd. Here, there is a sense of haste and sometimes danger.
G1599.origine: The word is composed of "ek" (out of) and "pempo" (to send). It translates the Hebrew "shalah," which literally means "to let go, to send away." This composition (ek + pempo) emphasizes the idea of making someone leave, setting them on a journey outward, often with a mission or urgency. It is a classical Greek word, used for both official envoys and for people who are being sent away.
G1599.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament (Acts 13:4 and 17:10), but in two very revealing contexts. In Acts 13:4, it is God (through His Spirit) who sends His workers on a mission — a solemn moment in the missionary deployment of the early Church. In Acts 17:10, it is the believers themselves who use it to ensure the safety of those who are persecuted. In both cases, the word conveys a decisive action, often providential.
G1599.portee: This word reminds us that the apostles did not go of their own initiative, but were sent by God or by His Church. It also shows how the early Christians helped each other in danger. For today's believer, it is an invitation to recognize that our service comes from God and to support those who are in distress or on the front lines of faith.
